h: 6. Push with git, and preview a branch
b: This takes you from nothing to an app with a URL, a preview of a branch and a rollback, on your own computer, in about ten minutes. You need Git, a browser, and nothing else: no containers, no database and no proxy. Moorage downloads the toolchains an app needs by itself. 1. Install moor On macOS or Linux: In PowerShell on Windows 11: moor is one program: the server, and the command line that talks to it. The installer checks it against the release's checksums, needs no administrator rights, and starts nothing. Installing Moorage has everything else about it. 2. Start a server The local preset is for this computer only: plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1:8080, with apps at http://<app>.localhost:8080. Leave it running, and use another terminal for the rest. 3. Claim it moor server init printed a link, and moor server status shows it again. Open it, and create the first account, which is the server's administrator. The link is what stops anyone else from doing this first. Claiming a server creates its first account. The page then leads to Getting started in the console, which checks how the server is set up and watches for your first deployment. 4. Deploy an app The examples are complete apps, ready to deploy. Take the task list, which is FastAPI with a small database, and make it a repository of its own: Then deploy it: On the server's own computer, moor needs no sign-in. It says what it is doing as it does it (some lines are left out here): Nothing told it this is Python: it looked. It fetched uv and the Python the app asks for, checked them against their published checksums, installed the dependencies from uv.lock, ran the migrations in the app's moorage.toml, and moved the traffic once the new instance answered its health check. Open http://tasks.localhost:8080. Chromium- and Firefox-based browsers find *.localhost addresses by themselves; for Safari and the command line, moor server resolver install sets that up. The console, at http://moorage.localhost:8080, shows the same thing with more to look at: An app's page: how it stands, what it has been doing, and what runs. 5. Change it, and go back A variable is part of a release, so changing one releases it, in less than a second and without downtime: Going back needs no build either, since the builds of recent releases are kept: A rollback is a new release of an earlier build, so that the record stays in order: It runs with the variables you have now. Releases, rollbacks and scaling says more. 6. Push with git, and preview a branch Add the server as a remote, and pushing deploys. The push shows the build, and fails if the deployment does: Any other branch gets a place of its own, with its own address, data and releases. Make a change on a branch: In tasks/static/index.html, change What needs doing? to something else, then: That build took just over half a second, as the toolchains and packages were already there. Open the address, and it asks you to sign in: a preview is for those with a role in the app, unless you say otherwise. An app's environments, each with its own address and release. Delete the branch, and the preview goes with it: Previews and environments has staging, promoting, locks and sleeping. 7. See how it is running The console has the same as it happens. An app's Logs tab follows and searches what it says, and Metrics charts its requests, response times, CPU and memory, with each release marked: What an app says, as it says it. 8. Clean up This stops the server and every app on it: To remove everything, delete ~/.moorage as well (%LocalAppData%\Moorage on Windows). To keep trying things, start it again with moor server run: everything is as you left it. Where to go next Your own app: run moor deploy in its directory. Moorage works out Go, Python, Node.js and static sites by itself, and runs anything else or a container if you say how. moor manifest explain shows what it would do. The words Moorage uses: Concepts has them on one page. A server for your team: install it as a service, with its own domain and certificates, then add people. Running a server says what to set up in the first week. Deploying from GitHub, GitLab or Gitea: connect a repository, and each pull request gets a preview.

The words the rest of this documentation uses, and how the things they name fit together. An app, its environments, and what each one runs. The server The server is the moor program, run as a service on one machine. It keeps its state in one SQLite database and one data directory, and answers every app's hostname itself. There is nothing else to install, and no cluster: Moorage is one machine, done well. The same program is also the command line you use from your own computer, which talks to the server through its API. The web console is part of the server, and shares its code with the API. Apps An app is what you deploy, usually one repository. Its name becomes part of its address: tasks is served at tasks.apps.example.com. Its moorage.toml, the manifest, says how to build and run it, and is optional when Moorage can work that out for itself. Environments An environment is a place where an app runs, with its own address, variables, data directory and releases. What it is Address Production What the app is for. Every app has it tasks.apps.example.com A named environment A place that stays, such as staging tasks--staging.apps.example.com A preview A branch, made by pushing it, and gone when it goes tasks--new-title.apps.example.com Previews and environments has the details. Builds, releases and deployments A build is what comes out of building one version of the source: a directory, or a container image. It does not change afterwards. A release is a build and a set of variables, numbered v1, v2 and so on in each environment. Whatever changes what runs makes a new one: a deploy, a change of variables, a rollback or a promotion. So the list of releases is the history of what an environment ran, and going back to any of them takes a moment. A deployment is the job that makes a release: build, or take a build there is already, run the release command, and roll it out. It succeeds or fails, and if it fails, the release before it goes on serving. See Releases, rollbacks and scaling. Processes and instances A process is a kind of thing an app runs, named in its manifest. web gets the app's traffic, and an app may also have others, such as worker, that do not. An instance is one running copy of a process. Each is watched by a small supervisor that restarts it if it fails, and that keeps it running while the server itself restarts or is upgraded. A static site has no processes at all: Moorage serves its files. A cron job and a one-off command run as short-lived instances of the current release, with its variables and data (more). Variables and secrets Variables are what an app is configured with, kept on the server and given to it as its environment. A secret is a variable sealed with the server's master key, which is handed to the app in memory and is not shown again (more). Changing either makes a new release, unless you ask to keep the change for the next deploy. Data The data directory of an environment survives deploys, and is at $MOORAGE_DATA_DIR. Everything else about a release is read-only once built, which is why an app's own files belong in that directory (more). It suits a SQLite database, with a dump for backups. For anything else, Moorage can run PostgreSQL or object storage for an app, or you can reach your own through a variable, such as DATABASE_URL. Gates A gate says who can reach an environment: anyone, whoever has a password, people signed in, or only those with a share link. It can also be limited to a list of addresses (more). Projects, roles and tokens Every app belongs to one project, and people have a role in a project: Role What it adds Viewer Sees apps, status and metrics, and usually logs Deployer Deploys, restarts, rolls back, promotes, scales, and makes previews and share links Maintainer Changes variables, secrets, domains and gates, and members; deletes apps Administrator Everything on the server: settings, users, every project, and the audit log. This one is a role on the server, and not in a project An API token lets a script act as you, within the scope you give it: read, deploy, admin or gate. It can also be limited to one app, and made to expire (more). Deploying is running code on the server, so treat it like shell access: Security says what that means. Runtimes and drivers A runtime is how an app is built and started: Go, Python, Node.js, static, a command of your own, a Containerfile, or an image. Moorage detects the common ones. Most run as ordinary processes on the server, and those in containers run under Podman or Docker. Nothing else needs an engine. Toolchains are what the native runtimes are built with: Go, Node.js, uv and Python. Moorage downloads each one the first time an app asks for it, checks it, and keeps it per version, so that every app gets the version it asked for.

h: For each app: add the remote, push
b: Every app has a git repository on the server. Pushing its production branch deploys it: the build is shown in your terminal as it happens, and the push fails if the deploy does. Once: register your SSH key That registers ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (or id_ecdsa.pub, or id_rsa.pub; name another file to use it) on your account. Moorage accepts Ed25519, ECDSA and RSA keys of 3072 bits or more. moor keys lists yours, moor keys remove NAME removes one. A push is recorded as yours, and until projects arrive, any account may push to any app. For each app: add the remote, push In the app's repository: moor git remote adds a remote named moorage, for the app named by [app].name in moorage.toml (or --app, or the directory's name), such as ssh://git@moorage.apps.example.com:2222/hello.git. The app need not exist: the first push creates it. The first time, ssh asks you to trust the server's host key: its fingerprint is in the server's log, on the line that starts the SSH listener (git pushes over SSH … host_key=SHA256:…). Once the remote is there, the other commands find the app from it: moor logs -f, moor rollback and the rest need no --app. What a push does Push What happens The production branch Deployed to production. The production branch is the repository's default branch: main, or, if the first push had no main, the first branch it pushed. A branch named in [environments.NAME] Deployed to that environment. Another branch Deployed to a preview of its own, at its own address. A tag Kept, not deployed. git push moorage --delete BRANCH The branch is deleted, and its preview destroyed; the production branch cannot be. A commit whose message contains [skip deploy] Kept, not deployed. What touches nothing in watch of [app], or moorage.toml Kept, not deployed. A locked environment takes no deployments: the commits are kept, and not deployed, and the push says so. A failed deploy fails the push. The deploy runs before the branch moves: if it fails, git reports the push as rejected, with the deployment's ID and why, and the branch on the server stays where it was. Fix the problem and push again. The previous release keeps serving meanwhile. Ctrl-C leaves the deploy running. Follow it with moor deployments follow ID; the branch moves if it succeeds. Force pushes are accepted: Moorage is where you deploy, not where the code is kept. Two pushes to one branch do not deploy at once: the second is refused until the first has finished. Pushes to different branches, or apps, go on side by side. Push options git push -o OPTION changes one push: Option Effect skip-deploy Keep the commits without deploying them. detach Accept the push at once; the deploy goes on (follow it with moor deployments follow ID). env=NAME Deploy this branch to that environment, which must exist, whatever the branch's name. Over HTTPS Where SSH is blocked, push over HTTPS with the API token: The remote is https://moorage.apps.example.com/git/hello.git, and moor git remote --http sets up moor git credential for it, a git credential helper that gives git the token of the server moor talks to. The token is not given to any other host, and not stored in a keychain. In a script, use an API token as the password (Accounts and access): pushing needs the deploy scope, fetching the read scope, and a token restricted to an app reaches only that app's repository. A disabled user's keys and tokens stop working at once. What is deployed The commit's files, as moor deploy would upload them: what .moorignore excludes is left out, and so are node_modules, .venv and __pycache__. Symbolic links and submodules are left out, and the push says so. Git LFS is not supported: the app gets the pointer files, and the push warns. moor deployments shows what each push deployed: Limits A push may be up to 1 GiB. git push --atomic is not supported, and a failed deploy refuses every ref of the push it belongs to. The repository can be cloned and fetched (git clone ssh://…/hello.git), with the same keys and token. listen.ssh in server.toml sets the SSH port (2222 by default); set it to "" to turn SSH pushes off.

h: When the server has been away
b: What this has been tried against. GitHub, by hand, with a real repository and a real token: polling, a private repository, pushes, a named environment, pull requests with their previews, checks and comments, approval, and catching up after being away. CI does the same with GitLab and Gitea in containers on each change to this code, a real fork's pull request included. Two things have not been tried on GitHub itself: delivery to a server that it reaches directly, as the deliveries were replayed from its own log, and a real fork, as that one's payload was edited to say so. If you try them first, please say how it goes. Connect an app to a repository on GitHub, GitLab or Gitea, and what happens there deploys here: A push to the default branch deploys to production. A push to a branch that an environment names deploys to that environment. Each pull request gets a preview of its own, which goes away when the pull request closes. If the server has a token, a check on the commit and one comment on the pull request say how that went, and where the preview is. A pull request from a fork, or from someone the forge does not say may push there, waits for someone to approve it. Pushing to Moorage with git push goes on working, for whoever may. The next change on the forge to that branch takes its place, so it is simplest to choose one or the other for each app. Connecting a repository Make the app, and connect it, from its folder or with --app: An app's Settings connects a repository, as well as moor forge connect does. Or in the console, in the Repository section of the app's Settings. The repository is given by its https address, and the address of anything other than github.com or gitlab.com needs --kind gitea, --kind gitlab, --kind github or --kind generic to say what it is. The default branch, which deploys to production, is what the repository says, and follows it if that changes, unless --branch says which and keeps it there. Connecting answers with an address and a secret, for the forge's webhook. The secret is shown this once. Connecting again to change something leaves both as they are; to have another secret, disconnect, connect, and give the forge the new ones. Connecting deploys nothing. The next push does, or: moor forge says how the connection stands, including what went wrong with the last thing that it heard of. The webhook Forge Where What to set GitHub Repository, Settings, Webhooks The address as the payload URL, application/json, the secret, and the events Pushes and Pull requests GitLab Project, Settings, Webhooks The address as the URL, the secret as the secret token, and the triggers Push events and Merge request events Gitea Repository, Settings, Webhooks The address as the target URL, application/json, the secret, and the events Push and Pull Request The forge has to be able to reach the server's console hostname. If it cannot, see looking for changes. The token Without a token, Moorage can read a public repository and deploy from it, and it says nothing back. A token reads a private repository, and sets the checks and comments. It is kept sealed, and is not shown again. Forge What it needs GitHub A fine-grained token for the repository: Contents to read, Commit statuses and Pull requests to read and write GitLab A project access token with the api scope, as a Maintainer: a Developer cannot set a check on a protected branch, such as the default one Gitea A token with read:repository, write:repository and write:issue A token only goes to the forge it was given for. Changing the repository's address, or --api-url, without giving a token again leaves the connection with none. Nor is a token sent in the clear across the internet: an address that is not https has to be on the local network for one to be accepted. A repository that has been renamed has to be connected again by its new address, as a forge sends anything else there by a redirect, which this server does not follow. A forge of your own For a forge at its own hostname, --kind says which kind it is, and its API is expected where that kind's API usually is. --api-url says otherwise, and a token is held to the same for it. --kind generic is any git server that can sign a webhook: it sends JSON with ref and after or commit, and an HMAC-SHA256 of the body, in hexadecimal, in X-Moorage-Signature. It has no pull requests, and nothing to report back to. Moorage reaches a forge as it reaches a webhook, so an address on this machine or a link-local one is refused unless [notifications] allow names it. Pull requests A pull request's preview is an environment named after its number, such as pr-42, at an address of its own. Its checks are called moorage, which a branch protection rule can require. Each new commit takes the place of the last, and the same comment says so. Closing the pull request or merging it takes the preview away. With a connection that hears of pull requests, branches do not get previews for being pushed, as what is in a pull request would be built twice. --no-previews leaves pull requests alone, and then only the default branch and those that an environment names deploy. A pull request's manifest has no say in where it goes: naming an environment for itself would not take it there, and [previews] branches is about branches. It can have no preview, with [previews] enabled = false, [skip deploy] or [app].watch, and it can say who may reach its preview with [previews] access, as any commit's manifest can. Code from strangers Building a pull request runs its code on this server, and its preview has the app's variables for previews. So one is not built for being opened if it comes from a fork, or if the forge does not say that its author may work there. On GitHub that means an owner, a member or a collaborator. A private member of an organization looks to the server like anyone else, and has to be approved or make their membership public. On GitLab and Gitea, anything in the repository itself counts, as pushing ther

Moorage builds a Go app from its source with the Go version its go.mod asks for, and runs the binary. The app The app listens on 127.0.0.1 and the port in $PORT: No manifest is needed: a go.mod is enough. A moorage.toml names the app and a health check: Deploy See what Moorage will do, then do it: The build is shown as it happens: the Go toolchain is downloaded (once, and verified against its published checksum), the app is built with go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w', and the new release takes over once it answers its health check. How it builds Go version: the toolchain line of go.mod, or else the newest patch release of the go line's version (go 1.26 builds with the newest 1.26.x). [go].version overrides both. Builds run with GOTOOLCHAIN=local. Main package: the top directory when it is package main, or else the single ./cmd/* with one; set [go].main otherwise. The binary is named after the module (or the main package) and placed in $MOORAGE_BIN; [go].binary renames it. cgo is off; [go].cgo = true turns it on (the server then needs a C compiler). [go].tags and [go].ldflags pass build tags and linker flags. Modules and the build cache are shared between builds, so later builds are quick. [build].command replaces the build entirely, and [build].pre and [build].post run before and after it. Running it A web process gets PORT and HOST=127.0.0.1. Moorage sends it a TERM signal to stop, then kills it after 30 seconds (stop_timeout). The app runs in its build directory, whose files are read-only. Write data to $MOORAGE_DATA_DIR, which survives deploys. More processes, such as a worker run by the same binary, go under [processes] (a process that does not listen on PORT counts as healthy once it has run for five seconds): Logs, restarts and rollbacks work the same for every app: A complete app: the Links example, a link shortener with only the standard library.

Moorage builds Python apps with uv: it installs the Python version the project asks for and the project's dependencies into a virtual environment, in the directory the app runs from. The app A FastAPI app, for example, with its dependencies in pyproject.toml and locked in uv.lock (uv lock): Moorage finds the app object — in main.py, app.py, server.py, asgi.py, wsgi.py or api.py, or in those files of a package at the top (a directory with an __init__.py) — and runs uvicorn main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port $PORT. A Django or Flask app with gunicorn among its dependencies is found the same way, and a project with a single [project.scripts] entry runs that script. Otherwise, say what to run in moorage.toml: Deploy How it builds Python version: .python-version, or else requires-python, or else the newest release; [python].version overrides them. A partial version (3.13) means its newest patch release. Dependencies: uv sync --locked --no-dev with a uv.lock (a lock that does not match pyproject.toml fails the build), uv sync --no-dev without one (with a warning), or for a requirements.txt, a virtual environment and uv pip install -r requirements.txt. [python].groups and [python].extras install more. The virtual environment's bin comes first on PATH, so python, uvicorn and the project's scripts are found without uv run. VIRTUAL_ENV is set, and PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, so that output reaches the logs at once. uv's cache is shared between builds. The release command [release].command runs once per deployment, after the build and before the new release takes traffic, with the release's variables: database migrations go there. If it fails, the deployment fails and the previous release keeps serving. It does not run on a rollback or a change of variables. [release].on_create runs once, after an environment's first release (to seed data). Two traps of http.server Apps built on the standard library's http.server: Use ThreadingHTTPServer, not HTTPServer: the latter answers one connection at a time, and an idle connection from Moorage's proxy then holds up every other request. HTTPServer looks up the name of the address it binds. On some machines that reverse lookup of 127.0.0.1 takes half a minute, and each new instance takes as long to start. Override server_bind, as the sample in testdata/apps/python does. Production servers (uvicorn, gunicorn, hypercorn) have neither problem. A complete app: the Tasks example, FastAPI with a web page, SQLite and migrations.

Moorage builds Node.js apps with npm, with the Node.js version the project asks for, and runs the start script — or serves the build's output as a static site when there is none. The app A build script, if there is one (tsc, vite build…), runs after the install. Commit package-lock.json (npm install makes it). A moorage.toml is optional: Deploy How it builds Node.js version: .nvmrc, or else .node-version, or else engines.node, or else the current LTS release; [node].version overrides them. Partial versions (24) and ranges (>=22, ^22.1, 24.x, lts/*) are resolved to the newest matching release (a >= range prefers LTS releases). Dependencies: npm ci (or npm install, with a warning, without a lockfile), then the build script if there is one ([node].build_script names another), then npm prune --omit=dev ([node].prune = false keeps development dependencies). pnpm, yarn and bun are not available yet; to use one installed on the server, set [build].command and toolchains = ["pnpm@system"] under [app]. node_modules/.bin comes first on PATH, and npm's cache is shared between builds. Running it The start script runs directly — not through npm start — so that the stop signal reaches the app. NODE_ENV=production is set. Without a start script, the build's dist/, build/ or out/ (the first with an index.html) is served as a static site, with the rules of [static] (see static sites): single-page apps set spa = true. A complete app: the Poll example, an Express API with a Vite front end.

b: A directory of files — documentation, a report, a single-page app — is served as it is, from Moorage itself: no process runs for it. Upload a directory Every deploy is a new release, swapped in at once; moor rollback brings the previous one back in a moment. Or drop its folder in the console On an app's Deploy page, drop a folder on the box at the top, or choose one. It goes up and is live a moment later, with nothing to install, and a new app that way is made for it as well. An app's Deploy tab. What is in one folder is taken to be the site, so that site/index.html is the front page. .git, .env, .env.* and the clutter that operating systems leave are left out, since whoever drops a folder does not see what is hidden in it, and the deployment's log says what was. A moorage.toml at its top says how to serve it, as below, and who may reach it, and is not served itself. A folder with a moorage.toml for an app that builds or runs is refused, as it would serve that app's source: upload that as source instead. Or build it From source, Moorage detects a static site when the directory has an index.html (at the top or in dist, build, out, public, _site or site), and runs a build command first if you give one: A Node.js project without a start script is served the same way, from the output of its build (see Node.js). Every release at its own address Each release of a static site that is still kept can be seen at an address of its own, as it was when it was deployed, to compare versions or to show someone an exact build: moor releases lists them, and the view link in an app's Deployments goes to them. This takes a certificate for those addresses. A server that gets one for each hostname from a CA does not ask for them, since anyone could then spend the CA's limit for your domain by visiting them, so that it does not offer them either. A wildcard covers them. The other ways of getting a certificate do too. They are behind the gate that the environment has now, so that closing an environment closes its old releases too, and they tell search engines to stay away. Moorage keeps an app's last five releases, or as many as keep_releases says. They need the same wildcard DNS record as the rest of your apps, so that with path routing there are none. Serving rules [static] says how files are served: Files whose names carry a content hash (app.3f2a9c1b.js) are cached as immutable, HTML is revalidated, and pre-compressed .br and .gz files are served to browsers that accept them. listing = true lists directories, for file shares. Files and directories whose names start with a dot are as good as absent, since .env and .git are far more often left behind than meant to be served. .well-known is the exception, and dotfiles = true serves the others. A complete site: the Handbook example, with clean URLs, a 404 page, headers and redirects.

Moorage runs most apps directly, with a toolchain it installs. An app runs in a container when it brings its own image: a Containerfile or Dockerfile to build, or an image that is built already. It is deployed, released, rolled back, routed and logged like any other app. The server needs Podman or Docker. No other app needs either. From a Containerfile With a Containerfile or Dockerfile and no go.mod, pyproject.toml or package.json, nothing else is needed: A language's own files come first in detection: to build the image of an app that has them, say so. The engine keeps its layers, so the next build is quicker. git push works the same way. A complete app: the Guestbook example, with a multi-stage build and an image holding one binary. Variables flagged for builds (moor env set --build) reach the build as build arguments, for the ARG lines that name them. Remember that an image's history keeps its build arguments: don't pass a secret this way to an image anyone else will see. From an image The server pulls the image and records its digest. Restarts and rollbacks run exactly that image, whatever the tag has come to mean since; deploying the same tag again picks up what it means now. An image on the server only, that no registry has, is used as it is. The moorage.toml in the current directory goes with it, if there is one, and no other file. Or name the image there, and moor deploy needs no flag: Private registries The server signs in with credentials an admin gives it, kept encrypted with its master key: The password is asked for, or read from standard input. Nothing checks it until the next pull. It reaches the engine in a temporary file, readable only by the server's user, for as long as the pull takes; it is used for private base images too. moor registry lists the registries and moor registry logout HOST removes one. What runs Command What the image says to run. A command under [processes] replaces it, entrypoint and all. Plain and shell commands A command of plain words runs directly, so an image needs no shell for it: /app/server --port 8000. Anything else ($PORT, &&, quotes) runs in the image's /bin/sh. Port port under [container], or else the lowest port the image EXPOSEs, or else 8080. $PORT is set to it, and the app must listen on all addresses: $HOST is 0.0.0.0. Publishing On the server's loopback interface only, on a port Moorage chooses. Traffic arrives through the router. User user under [container], or else whoever the image says. Data The environment's data directory at /data, or mount under [storage], as $MOORAGE_DATA_DIR. It survives deploys. Variables [env], the app's variables and secrets, and Moorage's. Nothing else comes from the server: PATH, HOME and the rest are the image's. Limits [resources]: memory, CPU and processes, for each instance. Privileges no-new-privileges, and no host network or privileged mode. An init process reaps zombies and passes on signals. The release command, and on_create, run in a container of the new image, with the same variables and data directory, and no port. So do workers: every process under [processes] is a container of the same image. Running them moor ps, moor logs, moor restart and moor rollback work as for any app. Moorage owns restarts, by restart under [processes]. The engine's own restart policy is off, and a container that keeps exiting is restarted more and more slowly. One the kernel killed for running out of memory says so in its log and in moor ps --json, where the engine reports it. Podman 4.9 does not: the log says the container was killed, perhaps for going over its memory limit. A health check needs an answer. A published port accepts connections whatever the container is doing, so a TCP check also waits to see that the connection stays open: a health.path is still the better check. Containers outlive the server. A restarted server finds them by their labels and takes them over, and their output in between is in their log. After a reboot, they are started again. Each is a command you could run yourself. Moorage calls the engine's command line. Its containers are named moorage-<app>-<env>-<process>-<n>-<id> and labelled io.moorage.*, so podman ps --filter label=io.moorage.app=guestbook finds an app's. Removing one is noticed, and the instance is replaced. Choosing the engine Under [containers] in server.toml: auto is whichever of Podman and Docker is answering, or else the first one found. Otherwise, name a binary. The engine runs as the server's user, with its usual settings: CONTAINER_HOST and DOCKER_HOST in the server's environment are honoured. The engine Only an app that runs in a container needs one. The server asks as it starts, without waiting for the answer, and says what it found in its log. A server with apps in containers waits a few seconds for it, and what it cannot find out in that time waits for the engine. After that it asks when something needs the engine, such as deploying one of those apps, and when someone looks at how the server stands, keeping the answer for half a minute. An app that does not run in a container never causes it to ask. It finds Means What happens Absent No program to run The server and every other app carry on. Deploying what needs an engine says to install one Not answering A program with no daemon or machine behind it, such as Docker Desktop not started or podman machine stopped The same, and it says to start it Ready It answered Apps can run in containers So you can start Docker Desktop an hour later, or install Podman, with no restart. A daemon that goes down does not make Moorage think that what it was running has stopped: once it answers, the same containers carry on. While it is down, deploying, restarting, scaling, rolling back, putting such an app to sleep or deleting it says why it cannot, and changes nothing. If it stops answering while apps need it, server.engine_down says so, to the rules that ask. A container that could not be stopped is stopped once the engine ans

Moorage runs anything that serves HTTP on a port: say how to build it, if it needs building, and what to run. Build on the server The command runtime runs your build command, with extra toolchains on the PATH — installed by Moorage (go, node, python, uv) or, with @system, the server's own: A Procfile (web: … lines) can stand in for [processes]. Run it as it is The binary runtime runs the uploaded files without building them — a script for an interpreter on the server, for instance: To upload something you built elsewhere, such as in CI, deploy the build's output with --artifact and the [processes] of the moorage.toml in the current directory: gRPC A gRPC server speaks HTTP/2 with no TLS, and nothing else, so say so: Clients reach it at its address like anything else. With TLS, they use https as a browser would, and with no TLS, as on your own computer, they speak HTTP/2 from the first byte. Streams work in both directions, and trailers come through, which is where gRPC says how a call went. Moorage reads none of it, so that a failed call is still a 200 in the metrics, and its gates apply as they do to anything: a sign-in gate means a browser's sign-in, which is no use to a program, so an API token or public suits a gRPC server better. The health check is a TCP connection to $PORT by default. health.path asks a path over HTTP/2, for a server that answers one, and a server with only gRPC services has none. Behind a proxy, the proxy has to speak HTTP/2 to Moorage: with nginx, that is grpc_pass to the plain port. What every app gets PORT to listen on, and HOST=127.0.0.1: apps are reached only through Moorage. MOORAGE_DATA_DIR, a directory that survives deploys, and MOORAGE_APP, MOORAGE_ENV, MOORAGE_RELEASE, MOORAGE_URL and others describing where it runs. A health check: a TCP connection to PORT, or with health.path, an HTTP request that must answer 2xx or 3xx. A new release takes traffic only once every instance is healthy; until then the previous one keeps serving. Commands are run by a POSIX shell built into Moorage, the same on every system; a simple command (a program and its arguments) is run directly. The programs they call must exist on the server. The stop signal (TERM, or stop_signal), then a kill after stop_timeout (30 seconds). Processes that exit are restarted, more and more slowly if they keep crashing.

The console is at the server's console hostname: https://moorage.apps.example.com, or http://moorage.localhost:8080 on your own computer. Sign in with your account; moor server status shows the link that creates the first one. Nearly everything in it is also available from moor or the API. Getting started Claiming a server leads here, and Getting started in the sidebar comes back. It says how the server looks (its DNS and certificates, for an admin), what to install and how to sign in from your own computer, and how to deploy. It watches for your first deployment, and says when it is live. Apps Every app: how it stands, its address, its release and its last deployment, changing as they do. New app asks for a name and a project, and says how to deploy it. Filter the list by typing part of a name. Each has a little line of its requests over the last hour. Every app, changing as they do. Status Healthy Every instance is healthy 1 of 2 healthy Some are not, and those that are get the traffic Down None is Deploying A deployment is under way Live A static site being served Sleeping Nothing used it for a while, so its instances are stopped, and the next request wakes it Scaled to zero It was asked to run no instances Deploy failed Its first deployment failed, so that nothing is served Not deployed It has never had a release A badge beside the status says if the latest deployment failed, while the release before it keeps serving. An app Its page says what it serves and who deployed it, lists its instances with their health, restarts and last exit, and shows its latest deployments and activity. Instances and deployments change as they do. From here: An app's page. Deploy Says how: from its directory, with git push, or from the page, by uploading a .tar.gz of its source or naming an image. It goes to the deployment when one starts. moor deploy Redeploy Builds again what the current release was built from: the same commit, upload or image name, for when a toolchain has moved, a tag points elsewhere or a build variable has changed. A release uploaded ready to run has nothing to build. moor redeploy Restart Replaces the instances, without downtime, or those of one process. moor restart [PROCESS] Roll back Serves the release before this one again, as a new release, in seconds. A deployment's page rolls back to that one, and can restore the variables it ran with. moor rollback Scale Says how many instances of each process run. moor scale Sleep and Wake Stops its instances until a request wakes it, and starts them again. moor sleep, moor wake When an app has more than one environment, its pages have a choice of which one at the top, and everything on them is about that one. An app's Settings are for maintainers: moving it to another project, renaming it, deleting it, and connecting a repository, which shows its pull requests and approves them. Renaming changes its address and git remote. Its instances stop and start again under the new name, so there is a moment of downtime. Change [app].name in its moorage.toml and its git remote to match: a deploy by the old name makes a new app. Deleting stops its instances and removes its variables, releases, builds, logs and repository, and its data directory unless you keep it. The page says how much each takes, and asks you to type its name. Scale on an app's page says how many instances of each process run. See Scaling. Environments and previews An app's Environments tab lists where it runs: each with its status, address and release. From here you make an environment or a preview of a branch, Promote what one runs to production, Lock one against deployments, Pin a preview and Remove or Destroy what you no longer need. Previews, in the sidebar: those of every app you can see. Previews in the sidebar has those of every app you can see, with when each was last used and when it expires. Metrics An app's Metrics tab has charts of its requests, response times, CPU and memory, for the chosen environment, from the last few minutes to the last 30 days, with each release marked. The last hour on its page has them at a glance. Cron An app's Cron tab lists its cron jobs, with their schedules, when each next runs and how it last went, and Run now does just that. Below them are its runs, each with what it said, and a box to run a command in the current release. Domains and access An app's Domains and access tab has hostnames of your own for the chosen environment, with the DNS record each needs and whether it points here. It says who can reach the environment, and why, and for maintainers changes it: anyone, a password, those signed in, or only share links, and a list of addresses. Below it, deployers make and revoke share links, each shown only when it is made. A deployment Its page shows how it is going, as it goes: A deployment, with its stages and log. Stages: prepare, toolchains, build, release and rollout, with how long each took, and those it did not need. A rollback needs no more than a rollout. The log, as it is written, with what went wrong if it failed. What changed since the release before it: whether the build did, the lines of the resolved manifest, and which variables were added, changed or removed. Of variables it shows the names, never their values. The resolved manifest: what moor manifest explain says, for this build. Logs An app's Logs tab shows what it says, as it says it: the output of every instance, merged by time. You can narrow it down by instance, time, text and source, and pause, go further back or download it. See Logs. Variables An app's Variables page lists what it runs with, and where each comes from: this environment, every environment, or the [env] of its moorage.toml, which a variable set here overrides. A secret is sealed when it is set, and is never shown again. Edit as text, for pasting a .env or changing many at once. Add a variable or Change one, and the change is released at once, as a new release that runs without downtime; or Save wi

Every change to what an environment runs makes a new release: a build and a set of variables. This page says how a release takes over, what happens when one fails, and how to go back. What you do What it does Builds? Runs the release command? moor deploy, or a push Builds the source, and rolls it out Yes Yes moor env set The same build with the new variables No No moor rollback An earlier build, with the variables you have now No No moor promote --from staging The build another environment runs, with this one's variables No Yes moor redeploy Builds what the current release was built from again Yes Yes moor restart Replaces the instances of the current release, and makes no new release No No How a deployment goes A deployment's page, in the console. Its stages and log change as it goes. Prepare. It takes the source from the upload or the commit, and works out how to build it. Toolchains. It fetches what the build needs, the first time anything asks for that version. Build. It builds in the directory the release will run from, with [build] of the manifest, or as the runtime does. Release. It runs [release].command, if there is one, once, with the release's variables. Database migrations go here. If this fails, the deployment fails, and the release before it goes on serving. Rollout. New instances start, and take over. One deployment runs at a time in an environment. A newer one replaces any still waiting, so that the latest push wins, and builds across the server share a limit: half the CPUs by default. How a release takes over A rolling release: the old instances serve until the new ones are healthy. New instances start beside the old ones, each on a port of its own. Each is checked until it is healthy, for up to health.startup (60 seconds). With health.path it must answer that path with a 2xx or 3xx. Without it, a TCP connection to $PORT is enough, so give it a path if it matters. The traffic moves, all at once. The old instances finish their requests, for up to deploy.drain (30 seconds). Long-lived connections are closed at the end of that time. They get their stop signal, and are killed if they have not stopped after stop_timeout (30 seconds). So an app should stop cleanly on SIGTERM, and be able to run beside its previous version for a moment, as both are up during a rollout. Where that cannot work, strategy = "recreate" in [deploy] stops the old instances first, which means some downtime. A process that takes no traffic, such as a worker, overlaps in the same way: the new one starts, and then the old one stops. A static site has nothing to start. Its files are switched at once. When a deployment fails If the build fails, the release command fails, or a new instance does not become healthy in time, the new instances are stopped and the traffic never moves, so that with the default rolling strategy nobody using the app sees anything. The page says what went wrong, and shows the log: A failed deployment says which stage failed, and why. The app's page and the list of apps then show that its last deployment failed, beside the release that is still serving. A git push fails too, and says why, so that you need not go and look. Notifications can tell the people concerned. A deployment interrupted by the server restarting is marked as failed: deploy or push again. Rolling back That serves the release before this one again, as a new release, in about a second, as nothing has to be built. Name a release to go further back: It runs with the variables you have now, so that a secret you have since replaced stays replaced. To have those the earlier release ran with: The release command does not run again, and a rollback does not undo what a release did to its data. If a migration changed the database, the older code gets the newer database, so write migrations that the previous release can run beside. That is what it must do during a rollout anyway. In the console, Roll back on an app's page goes to the release before, and a deployment's page goes back to that one. Looking at releases diff says whether the build changed, which lines of the resolved manifest did, and which variables were added, changed or removed: their names, and never their values. Builds are kept for as long as one of an environment's last keep_releases releases (five, by default) uses them, and what an environment is running now is never removed. A release whose build has gone cannot be rolled back to, and the console says so. Scaling New instances start beside those running, and take traffic once they are healthy. Those beyond the number finish their requests and stop. If a new instance cannot start, the app goes back to how it was, and says why. The number stays, over the manifest's instances, through restarts and the releases to come, and the console says what the manifest would have had. 0 turns a process off, and 20 is the most. Requests are spread over the healthy instances. An instance holds nothing in common with another unless you arrange it, so that an app with more than one needs to keep what it shares somewhere they can all reach. An app that keeps something in memory for each visitor, as many keep a session, can ask to have each browser kept with one instance: Moorage does that with a cookie of its own, which the app does not hear, for as long as the browser is open. A browser moves to another instance when its instance is gone or unhealthy, as it is after every release, so that what was in memory is lost then: it makes an app work with several instances, and not safe to lose one. This is one machine: scaling lets an app use more of its CPUs, and does not add to them. Restarts and crashes An instance that exits is restarted, by the small supervisor that runs it, even while the server itself is away. The wait between restarts starts at a second and doubles, up to a minute. An instance that keeps failing, five times in ten minutes, counts as crashed, and is then restarted every five minutes. Those concerned are told

Variables configure an app without changing its code. They are set on the server and override the [env] of moorage.toml. An app's Variables tab says where each one comes from. Every change is a new release of the app's current build, rolled out like a deploy: new instances start with the new variables, take the traffic once healthy, and the old ones stop. Nothing is dropped. --no-restart keeps the change for the next deploy instead. Variables can be set before the first deploy. lists them with where each comes from (this environment, every environment, or moorage.toml) and which ones another source overrides. Secrets asks for the value without showing it (or reads it from standard input: moor env set --secret DATABASE_URL < url.txt), so it stays out of your shell's history. A secret is stored encrypted, listed without its value, handed to the app without being written to disk, and replaced by [secret] where the app, its build or its release command prints it (for values of six characters or more). A maintainer can read one back with moor env reveal NAME, which is recorded in the audit log. The key that encrypts secrets, keys/master.key in the data directory, must be backed up apart from the database. A server whose secrets were encrypted with another key, or without its key, refuses to start. What an app expects An app can say what it needs, with no values in the repository: A deployment that lacks one that is required fails early, saying which, before the app gets as far as falling over, and one that is secret must have been set as one. One to generate is made the first time it is needed, once for each environment, so that every preview gets its own. Rollbacks do not stop to check. moor env and the app's Variables page list them all, with their descriptions, and say what is missing. In other environments A variable belongs to one environment, or with --all-envs to all of them. A preview also inherits production's, and shows them as inherited; setting one of the same name on the preview overrides it. Keep one from previews with --production-only: More --all-envs sets a variable for every environment of the app; an environment's own variable of the same name wins. --build makes a variable available to builds too (a private package index token, for instance); it reaches the app with its next build. moor env unset NAME… removes variables. moor env import .env sets the variables of a .env file in one change (with --secret, all as secrets); moor env export writes the variables as a .env file, secrets as comments. moor rollback keeps the current variables; moor rollback --with-config restores the ones the earlier release ran with. PORT, HOST and the MOORAGE_* variables are set by Moorage and cannot be changed.

An app can run in more than one place at once, each with its own address, variables, data and releases. Those places are its environments: What it is Where it comes from How long it stays Production What the app is for Every app has it With the app A named environment, such as staging A place that stays [environments.staging], moor environments create, or moor deploy --env staging Until it is removed A preview A branch, to look at and to show Pushing a branch Until its branch goes, or nothing uses it for seven days Production is at shop.apps.example.com, and the others at shop--staging.apps.example.com. The double dash keeps the name one label, so that the one wildcard DNS record and certificate the server already has cover every environment of every app. Anything but production answers with X-Robots-Tag: noindex, so that search engines leave it alone, and each can have a gate of its own. Previews Push a branch: It is built from that branch, and each further push releases to it. Deleting the branch destroys it: Its name comes from the branch: lowercase, with anything else as a dash, at most 40 characters, with a short hash if it is cut or another branch has that name. Its variables are production's, except those marked as production's alone, then [environments.preview] of its moorage.toml, then any set on the preview itself. Keep a secret from previews when you set it: Who can reach it is, by default, those signed in with a role in the app's project, since it is work in progress with production's variables. Share links let in someone else, a maintainer can open one, and preview = "public" in server.toml opens them all. Its data starts empty: $MOORAGE_DATA_DIR is its own, and on_create in [release] runs once, to seed it. It runs what the branch says, with the number of instances production's manifest gives it, or [environments.preview] overrides. It sleeps when nothing has asked it for anything for 30 minutes, and wakes for the next request. It expires when nothing has deployed to it or asked it for anything for seven days, or what ttl says. Pin one to keep it. An app may have ten at a time; a push beyond that is kept and not deployed, and says so. A branch that was pushed while skipping the deploy can have a preview later: To choose which branches get one, or none: Named environments Declare one, and pushes to its branch deploy to it. Deploying the manifest that declares it makes it, and a first push of its branch does too: An app's Environments tab. Or make one yourself, and deploy to it however you deploy: Unlike most previews, a named environment inherits nothing of production's: it has the variables set for every environment (moor env set --all-envs), and its own. It has its own data directory, and it stays until it is removed, which takes a maintainer: Every command about one environment takes --env, and on an app's pages in the console the environment is chosen at the top. Promoting What runs in staging can go to production as it is, without being built again, in seconds: The build goes; the variables do not. It runs with those of the environment it goes to, and its own overrides in the manifest, and a release command runs as for any new build. If it was built with other build variables than that environment has, it says so: what it was built with stays in it, and moor redeploy builds it with these instead. Locks A lock stops deployments to an environment, so that a rollback, say, is not overwritten by the next push while you look into what went wrong. Pushes are kept, and not deployed. Rollbacks, variables, restarts and scaling go on working. The page of a rollback offers the lock. Once it is unlocked, the next push deploys, or moor redeploy builds what was kept. Sleeping An environment nobody is using need not use the machine. A preview goes to sleep after 30 minutes without a request, and any other environment does if you ask it to: Asleep, its instances are stopped; its address, data, logs and releases stay. A request wakes it and waits for it, so that the one who asked notices no more than a slow answer: A browser waits up to two seconds, and then gets a short page that says it is waking up, and reloads itself until it is ready. Anything else waits up to 30 seconds, and then gets a 503 with Retry-After. It does not go to sleep with a request still going on, such as a stream or a WebSocket. A process that must keep running, such as a worker that takes jobs from elsewhere, can say so, and stays up while the others sleep. A static site has nothing to stop, and never sleeps. Put one to sleep yourself, or wake one without waiting for a request. Deploying, restarting or scaling wakes it too: Who may do what Viewer Deployer Maintainer See environments and previews ✓ ✓ ✓ Make environments and previews, deploy, promote, lock, pin and put to sleep ✓ ✓ Destroy a preview ✓ ✓ Remove a named environment ✓ Inside an app An instance can tell where it is: Variable MOORAGE_ENV production, staging or feature-new-pricing MOORAGE_ENV_KIND production, named or preview MOORAGE_URL Its own address

Both run as one-off instances of an environment's current release: the same build, variables and data directory as its processes, for as long as the command takes. Cron jobs Declare them in moorage.toml, and they run from the next deployment: An app's Cron tab. Key Default name required Its name, unique in the app. schedule required Five fields (minute, hour, day, month, weekday), @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly, @yearly, or @every 15m. command required What to run. timezone the server's Such as Europe/Paris. timeout "1h" It is stopped after this long, a day at the most. overlap "skip" If the run before is still going: skip this one, allow both, or replace the one before. environments ["production"] Where it runs. "*" is every environment that stays; previews need naming, as "preview". A job that was due while the server was down waits for its next time. It runs in an environment that is asleep, without waking the rest of it. The last 100 runs of each job are kept, with what they said, how long they took and how they ended. A job that fails is in the activity. An app's Cron tab in the console has its jobs, with when each next runs and how it last went, and runs one now. One-off commands What follows -- runs as you gave it, word for word. One word is a command line, for the shell that Moorage has built in: What it says comes back as it says it, on standard output and standard error, and moor ends with its exit status, so that a script can tell. Interrupting moor stops the command. --detach leaves it running. It takes an hour at the most unless --timeout says otherwise, up to a day. A command that asks for input gets none, unless you are at a terminal, with -it. Running a command takes a deployer, as deploying does, and each is in the audit log. Secrets are kept out of what is recorded of its output. The Cron tab in the console has a box to run one, too. Inside a run $MOORAGE_PROCESS says what it is: cron-nightly-cleanup for a job, and run for a command. A release command, which runs with each deployment, says release.

Three ways of reaching an environment by hand, from the command line and from the console. What it is For moor run -it A terminal of your own, in a one-off instance A shell, a database prompt, anything that asks you things moor exec A command in a container that is running Looking at what that container has The Console tab One command at a time, in a browser When all you have is a browser moor files and the Files tab The environment's data directory Looking at, fetching and putting files All of them take being able to deploy to the app, as they can read what it keeps and act as it. Who started what, and who read which file, is in the audit log. What is done at a terminal after that is not. A terminal This starts a one-off instance of the current release, as moor run does, with its variables, its data directory, and its user and limits if the server keeps apps apart. You get a terminal of your own in it, the same size as yours, and it hears when yours changes size. All the keys go to what is running, Ctrl-C too. Leave as you would leave a shell. Losing the connection stops what was running, and all that it started that still has that terminal. Something that takes pains to leave it, such as a daemon, only goes with it where the server keeps apps apart with a cgroup. It takes an hour at the most, unless --timeout says otherwise, up to a day. moor ends with the command's own exit status. What is said in it is not kept, since a password can be typed into one. There is a record that it happened, of who ran what and how it ended, in the app's runs. Unlike the output of moor run, what a terminal shows has no secrets taken out. It would not be possible, and you could print them another way. With -i alone there is no terminal, only standard input, for feeding something to a command: On Windows, the terminal is a pseudo-console, and what it sends is understood by Windows Terminal and by anything else that understands the same escapes. A terminal takes an API token, which moor login gets you. A session in a browser cannot start one: any page you visit could ask your browser to open one, and it would send your cookies. Inside a running container A one-off instance is a new one. To see what a particular container has, give its instance, from moor ps: A command that is more than plain words goes through /bin/sh in the container, so an image with no shell can only run plain commands. What is running there belongs to the container: leaving stops moor's side of it, and a container engine may let the command go on until it ends or the container does. An app that is not in a container has nothing of its own to go into, as a process sees the same files from anywhere, and moor exec says so: moor run has them, with its variables and its user. The Console tab An app's Console tab, for those who can deploy to it, runs one command at a time and shows what it says as it says it. Each runs by itself: nothing carries over from one to the next, so a cd is forgotten, and it cannot ask you anything, as what it reads is empty. For those things, there is a terminal. An app's Console tab. The up and down arrows go back through what has been run. What a command says is kept with its run, with secrets taken out, as it is for moor run. The data directory Each environment has a data directory of its own, which is where its app keeps what it means to keep. An app's Files tab shows what is in it, with a preview of short text files, and can download, upload, make directories and remove. So can the command line: An app's Files tab. What is put there belongs to the app, and appears all at once, so that the app never sees half of it. In a container, where its user could be anyone, anyone may change it. It stops at something already there, unless told otherwise. Up to 1 GB, or moor run -i for more. Everything in there was written by an app, and is treated with that in mind. A link that leads out of the data directory is not followed, a pipe or a device is not opened, and someone else's file with another name elsewhere is not sent. A file is only ever sent as a download, and a preview is only ever text. Each of these is for an environment that is there: nothing can be put where an app of that name may find it later. Reading a file is in the audit log, as is anything that changes. There is no way back from removing something other than a backup.

Moorage captures what every instance writes to its standard output and standard error, with nothing to set up in the app. An app should just write to them, a line at a time. It also keeps its builds' logs, a log of the requests it served, and a record of what happened to it. In the console An app's Logs tab shows what it says, as it says it: the output of every instance, merged by time. An app's logs, following as they come. Instance: all of them, one process or one instance. When: the last 15 minutes up to the last 7 days, or between two moments. Search: the lines with this text, whatever its case, marked where it is. Sources: see below. Only problems: errors, warnings, standard error, and requests that failed. Pause stops the lines moving, and Resume brings what came meanwhile. Scrolling up holds the view where it is, and Newest lines comes back. Older lines goes further back, and Download gives you all of what is shown, up to 200,000 lines, as a file. From the command line Follow them, and narrow them down: Of the lines it prints, those marked * are Moorage's notes, and those marked ! came from standard error. --since takes how long ago (15m, 2h, 7d) or a moment, and --json prints each line as JSON for another program to read. Its --help has the rest. What there is Source What it is stdout, stderr What the app wrote moorage Moorage's notes of starts, exits and restarts, and why build The logs of its deployments access Its requests: who asked what, and how it went events What happened to it: deployments, restarts, changes of variables The first three show unless you ask otherwise. Lines with structure A line that is a JSON object reads as its message and fields, coloured by its level; hold the pointer over it in the console to see the line itself. A line of plain text that names a level, as ERROR: or level=warn, is coloured too, and both count for Only problems. So there is nothing to configure for structured logs: write one JSON object to a line. Secrets The values of an app's secrets are taken out of its output as it is captured, when they are six characters or more and appear as they are. It is a safety net, and not a reason to log them: a value that has been encoded or cut in two gets through. How long they are kept Of an instance running Until they rotate, at 10 MiB, with five files back Of an instance that has stopped 14 days Of a deployment For as long as its app and environment are there Of the events 90 days They are plain files, in logs in the data directory, so that tail and grep work on them too: Sending them elsewhere To keep them longer, or with everything else you run, send them on to syslog, an OpenTelemetry collector or any HTTP endpoint. What is kept here stays as it is.

Moorage keeps what your apps have been doing, with nothing else to run. An app's Metrics tab has it as charts, for each environment; The last hour on its page has it at a glance; and the list of apps has each one's requests. An app's Metrics tab. Chart What it is Requests a minute All requests, and those the app or Moorage failed (5xx). Response time How long 50% and 95% of them took, from when Moorage got them to when they ended. CPU By instance, in percent of one core, so that a process using two whole cores is at 200%. Memory By instance, and whatever each started. Each release is marked with its version on every chart, so that what changed lines up with what was deployed. Hold the pointer over a chart for its numbers, or tab to it and use the arrow keys. The numbers under each has them as a table, and every range works with no scripts at all. Only requests that got through a gate are counted. A connection held open as a WebSocket counts as a request, not as a response time. How long it is kept Every For In memory 10 seconds 2 hours In the database Minute 14 days In the database Hour 1 year A restart of the server loses what was in memory, which is at most the current minute's worth that had not been written. Percentiles stay right as they roll up, since it is histograms that are kept, and not averages of averages. A busy environment with two instances takes about 6 MB of database, all told. From the command line --range is live, 1h, 24h, 7d or 30d. With Prometheus The console's hostname answers at /metrics, with an API token that can read. It says only what the token's holder could see anyway, and what is of the server itself only to an administrator. Metric moorage_http_requests_total Requests, by app, env and status class moorage_http_response_bytes_total Bytes sent in answers moorage_http_requests_in_flight Requests going on now moorage_http_request_duration_seconds A histogram of how long they took moorage_instance_cpu_percent By instance_name, such as web.1, and process moorage_instance_memory_bytes The same. A service is one too, with an instance_name such as service.db moorage_host_load, moorage_host_memory_used_bytes, moorage_host_disk_used_percent The server itself Counts start again when the server does, as Prometheus expects of counters. How it is measured On Linux and macOS, an instance's usage is added up over its process and all that descend from it. Containers' usage comes from their engine. On Windows it is the same with what the system says of processes, and the server's load has no number there.

An app can ask for a database or an object store in its manifest, and Moorage runs it and connects the app to it. Each environment gets its own, so that a branch's preview has a database of its own to break. That is all it takes. On the next deployment, Moorage starts PostgreSQL 18 for that environment, waits for it to be ready, and then gives your app DATABASE_URL. A release command can migrate, as the service is ready before it runs. This is the one thing in Moorage, apart from apps in containers, that needs a container engine. Podman or Docker has to be there for an app that asks for a service, and nothing else cares. A deployment that asks for one with no engine answering says so before it builds anything. In the manifest Key Means Default type postgres or s3 Required version For postgres, 15 to 19 18. It is recorded when the service is made, and does not move by itself image For postgres, another image based on the official one, such as pgvector/pgvector:pg18, which is the way to get extensions. It needs a tag other than latest The official image env Another name for the variable, or for s3 the start of each, needed for a second of one type DATABASE_URL, or S3_ENDPOINT and its fellows memory A limit, such as 512MiB None previews own, or none for previews to have none own seed production, for a new preview to start with a copy. See what a preview starts with Empty sanitize With seed, a script in the app that removes what should not be copied, or none to say that nothing should Two of a type need different variables: An object store It gets one bucket, and one key that can do anything in it: Variable Is S3_ENDPOINT and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL Its address, such as http://127.0.0.1:27014 S3_BUCKET app S3_REGION and AWS_REGION us-east-1, which means nothing here and which clients want S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID Its key S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY Its secret key, kept out of what the app prints With env = "UPLOADS", they are UPLOADS_ENDPOINT and so on, and the AWS_ names are left for another. Clients need path-style addresses, as there is no name for a bucket to go in front of: force_path_style or addressing_style = "path", depending on the client. It is Versity Gateway, which keeps a bucket as a directory and an object as a file. Everyday S3 works: uploading in parts, presigned URLs, CORS and bucket policies. What does not: versioning, lifecycle rules, object ACLs, and keys a and a/b at once, as a file cannot also be a directory. An app that needs those needs real S3, which it can have by setting these variables on the environment itself, as below. A presigned URL is signed for its host, so that a browser elsewhere cannot use one for 127.0.0.1. For now, this is for what an app reads and writes for itself, and it has no public address. Which address an app gets From weakest to strongest: Variables for all environments, and what a preview inherits from production The address of this environment's own service A variable set on this environment itself So production can use a real database by setting its own DATABASE_URL, in which case Moorage starts nothing for it and needs no engine for it, while every preview still gets its own. A preview never ends up on production's database by inheritance: with previews = "none", what it would inherit of that name is left out. The address is given as an instance starts, as a secret is, along with its password alone as DATABASE_URL_PASSWORD. Neither is in a release or on a command line, and both are kept out of what the app prints. An app that runs natively gets 127.0.0.1 and a port that stays the same for the life of the service. One in a container reaches it by name, on a network for its environment. What happens to it When What happens You deploy It is made if it is not there, and started if it has stopped. If it does not become ready, the deployment fails, and the previous release goes on serving It stops by itself, or the machine restarts Moorage starts it again The server stops or is upgraded It goes on running, like your apps moor server stop --all or moor server uninstall It stops, after your apps, and keeps what it holds. The server starts it again when it next starts. Uninstalling says how to take it away The environment goes to sleep It stops, and keeps what it holds, unless a process with sleep = false or a command is still using it. Waking starts it first, and a command or a cron job starts it for as long as it runs The manifest stops naming it It stays, with what it holds, marked as unused. A release that does not name it does not get its address The environment is deleted It goes, with what it holds The engine stops answering What is running is left alone. Deploying, restarting, putting to sleep or deleting says why it cannot, and leaves what is running as it is. server.engine_down says so, to the rules that ask A manifest that asks for another major version than a service holds is refused, as that takes moving its data. PostgreSQL itself also refuses to start on a newer version's files, so this is not all that stands between a mistake and lost data. What a preview starts with Empty, unless the manifest says otherwise, with [release] on_create to put something in it, which runs once. Copying production into previews is how customer data leaks. To copy it anyway, it takes saying so, and saying what removes what should not be copied: A new preview then starts with production's latest dump, which a backup makes. The copy and the script happen where nothing can connect, and if either fails, or the server stops halfway, nothing is left of the copy, and the deployment fails. The script is in the app, and a link in its place that leads out of the app is refused. sanitize = "none" says that nothing needs removing. A preview starts empty all the same, and its deployment's log says why, if anyone can reach it, if it is the preview of a pull request that comes from a fork, or that nothing says does not, or if a coding agent's

Coding agents can deploy to Moorage and read how it went, through moor mcp or the command line. This page says how to connect one, what it can do, and what limits it. That makes a token that can only read, keeps it in a context of its own, and tells Claude Code how to run moor mcp. Connect a client moor mcp setup makes the token, and takes --client with any of the names here. Where a client has a command of its own, it runs that. Otherwise it says what to put where. With no --client, it lists them all, with the whole path to moor, as a desktop app does not start from your shell. Client --client It runs, or says to put Its documentation Claude Code claude-code claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope user moorage -- moor mcp MCP Codex CLI codex codex mcp add moorage -- moor mcp MCP VS Code vscode code --add-mcp with the server as JSON MCP Gemini CLI gemini gemini mcp add -s user moorage moor mcp MCP Cline cline cline mcp add moorage --yes -- moor mcp MCP Cursor cursor ~/.cursor/mcp.json MCP Antigravity CLI antigravity ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json MCP Devin Desktop, formerly Windsurf devin ~/.config/devin/mcp_config.json MCP Junie junie ~/.junie/mcp/mcp.json MCP Kiro, IDE and CLI kiro ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json MCP JetBrains AI Assistant jetbrains Settings, Tools, AI Assistant, Model Context Protocol (MCP) MCP Zed zed Its settings, under context_servers MCP Goose goose ~/.config/goose/config.yaml Extensions Claude Desktop claude-desktop claude_desktop_config.json MCP Kiro's IDE and kiro-cli read the one file, so that setting up either sets up both, and kiro-cli and kiro-ide are other names for --client kiro. moor mcp setup says what to put in that file. It does not run kiro-cli mcp add, which takes a server as one string and does not document how to give it the server's own flags. KIRO_HOME moves that file if you have set it. Kiro's autoApprove skips its prompts for the tools it lists, so that it is best to leave deploy, rollback and restart off. These were each read from the client's own documentation in November 2026, and these tools change quickly, so that their pages have the last word. Clients that take only a remote server, such as ChatGPT, cannot use it yet, as moor mcp runs on your own computer. The token goes in moor's own file, which only you can read, and in no client's configuration or repository. If a client runs on another computer or in a container, give it $MOOR_SERVER and $MOOR_TOKEN instead, with a token from moor tokens create. What it can do Tool Does Available list_apps, get_app What exists and how it stands Always list_deployments, get_deployment Stages, status and the end of the log Always read_logs The newest lines, filtered if asked Always list_releases What has run, and what can be gone back to Always check_manifest Checks a local moorage.toml, and says how Moorage would build and run the app Always deploy Uploads a directory, and returns at once with an id to ask about --allow-deploy rollback, restart Serves an earlier release again, or replaces what is running --allow-deploy Nothing here runs a command, reads a secret or deletes anything, and nothing manages domains, gates, members, tokens or the server. That is on purpose: a tool that runs commands would put what an app has written, its secrets and the way out all in one call. check_manifest and deploy read only below the directory that moor mcp started in, or --root DIR, with the same rules as moor deploy for what to leave out. They refuse if that directory is your home directory or above it, a directory that is hidden or ignored, and a tree with a link that leads out of it. If a client starts it somewhere else, say where to read from: Letting it deploy With --deploy, a token can deploy, roll back and restart, and only in previews, unless you say --envs all. Such a token: Deploys only to a name that starts with agent-, such as agent-new-pricing, which makes a preview of that name. The app has to exist already: create it yourself, with moor apps create. Can reach only those previews, for reading as well as changing. They take nothing of production's variables or those set for every environment, as the code it deploys could otherwise read them. A required variable has to be set on the preview by someone who can, with moor env set. Is refused anything else, including what is added to Moorage later. It cannot read production's logs, variables, files, deployments or runs, promote, change variables, lock or pin an environment, or read the app's events. Cannot use git, either to push or to clone, as a repository holds every branch. Is held to what any preview is: at most 10 to an app, and it expires after the usual time. What the code it deploys says in its manifest does not change that, or how many of production's releases are kept. What this does not do The token is the boundary, and nothing else here is. An agent with a shell can go around moor mcp altogether, and a tool's own description of itself is only advice to a client. So: Limiting a token limits what it can ask for, and code it deploys runs on your server. On Linux, an app's environments share a user, so that code in a preview can read production's data directory, and with no isolation it can read what the server can. To keep what an agent makes from production altogether, give it an app of its own, on a server where apps are kept apart, with --app. Logs are written by the app and whoever can reach it. An agent that reads them is reading what a stranger may have written, and could be told by it to do something. Moorage marks them, and removes what is hidden from view, which stops careless attempts and not determined ones. So keep what an agent can do small, and treat what it did after reading logs with care. A client's approval prompts help, and people approve nearly all of them, so that they are not the protection either. moor mcp refuses a token that can do everything, and does not fall back on what moor login stored, which never expires.
