Moorage says when something goes wrong: in the console for those it concerns, and through webhooks, chat and email for whatever you set up. An app that keeps crashing sends one message and not hundreds, and then a word when it has recovered. In the console Notifications in the sidebar has what you have been told, and how many you have not read. Nothing has to be set up. You are told: Notifications, in the sidebar. when a deployment of yours fails, whatever your role; when a deployment fails, an app keeps crashing or a cron job fails in a project you maintain, which includes a project whose Everyone else is maintainers; when the server's data volume is 90% full, if you are an administrator. Administrators are told of everything else as well. Notifications are kept for 90 days. From the command line: The server's local administrator, which is who moor is on the server's own machine until you sign in, is not an account, and has nothing to read. Channels A channel is somewhere word can go. Adding one takes an administrator, in Settings → Notifications or with moor notifications channels add. Settings → Notifications: its channels and rules. Kind What it sends webhook JSON, signed slack A message, to an incoming webhook teams A message, to an incoming webhook discord A message, to a webhook email A message, through your mail server That asks for the address of the webhook, since a chat webhook's address is a secret: --url gives it on the command line instead. Email has no address to ask for: That asks for the mail server's password, because --username says to sign in. Mail goes to port 587 unless --port says otherwise, using STARTTLS if the server offers it. Port 465 has TLS from the start. A password is only sent over TLS. All of what a channel needs is sealed with the server's master key. Afterwards only the webhook's host, or the addresses mail goes to, can be seen, and only by administrators. Those who are not administrators see a channel's name and kind, to choose it for a rule. See that one works: The list says when each channel last sent something, and why the last attempt failed if it did: Rules Nothing goes to a channel until a rule says so. A rule is for the whole server, a project or an app. A rule of the whole server takes an administrator, and one of a project or an app takes a maintainer of it, who can add it on the project's page or from the command line: A rule says what it wants. Without --events it has the first five of these: Event When deployment.failed A deployment fails instance.crashloop A process has exited three times in five minutes cron.failed A cron job fails server.disk_low The data volume is 90% full, which only a rule of the whole server hears server.certificate_failed A certificate from a CA could not be had or renewed, which only a rule of the whole server hears backup.failed A backup fails, which only a rule of the whole server hears server.engine_down The container engine stops answering while apps here need it, which only a rule of the whole server hears instance.unhealthy An instance fails its health check deployment.live A deployment goes live * asks for all of them. A channel told that something went wrong is told when it has come right: a deployment goes live after one that failed; a process that kept crashing has not exited for 10 minutes, or a new release has replaced it; all the instances that were unhealthy are healthy, or a new release has replaced them; the data volume is below 85%; a backup works after one that failed. One message, not hundreds What can happen over and over by itself is held back: after a message that a process keeps crashing, that an instance is unhealthy, that a cron job failed or that the disk is nearly full, others like it wait for 15 minutes, for the same environment and the same process or job. The next one after that says how many were held back. A word that it has recovered ends the wait, so that going wrong again is news at once, unless it keeps going back and forth, which is held back in the same way. In-console notifications go by the same rules. Deployments are not held back: each one is there because someone asked for it, and they are to hear how it went. A message that does not go is tried three times, ten and then twenty seconds apart. A message held up when the server stops is not sent afterwards. What happened is always in Activity, whatever became of the message. What a webhook sends type is one of the events above, or recovered, whose data.recovered_from says what from, or test. suppressed is how many like it were held back since the last that went. Anything but an answer of 2xx counts as not having gone, and redirects are not followed. Checking a webhook's signature Adding a webhook shows a secret, once. It signs each message, so that a receiver can tell that it came from your server, and came recently. The X-Moorage-Signature header has the time and an HMAC-SHA256, in hex, of the time, a dot and the body: To check it, work out the same from the body as it arrived, before parsing it: X-Moorage-Event has the message's type. What notifications may reach A channel's address could otherwise be used to reach what only the server can. So channels may not connect to this machine by any of its addresses, a link-local address or a cloud's metadata service, whatever name the address gives. Other addresses on your local network are allowed, since a team's own services are what many webhooks are for. Forges are held to the same. To allow more, name them in server.toml, and restart the server: The server connects directly, and does not use HTTP_PROXY or the like. See also Metrics, for how an app is doing all the time Projects and roles, for who maintains what Cron jobs

Each environment of an app has a gate, in front of everything it serves. Nothing behind it hears of those it turns away, whether it is a process or a static site. Gate Who gets through public Anyone. password Anyone with a password that you share. A browser gets a form, and is remembered for seven days. A script sends it with HTTP Basic. login People signed in to Moorage with a role in the app's project, or with --any-user anyone with an account. The app hears who they are. A script sends an API token with the gate scope. share Only people with a share link. Share links get through every gate, and a list of addresses can be combined with any of them. Which gate it has The first of these that says: An environment's gate, on its Domains and access tab. What a maintainer has set, in the console or with moor access set. What its manifest asks: access in [environments.NAME], or for previews in [previews]. A manifest is a deployer's, so it can ask for a gate where the server has none, and it cannot open what the server has closed: access = "public" then does nothing, and the app's page says so. What the server says of that kind of environment, in server.toml: Those are the defaults. A preview is work in progress, running with production's variables, so that it is not for everyone unless you say so: preview = "public" here opens them on this server, a maintainer can open one, and a link lets someone in. An environment's Access tab in the console says which it has and why, and changes it. So does this: A change takes effect at once. Changing the gate or its password ends the way in of everyone who was in. If its gate asks for a password nobody has set, nobody gets in until someone sets one. A password It asks for the password without showing it, or reads it from standard input. It must have at least 8 characters. A script sends it as the password of HTTP Basic, with any user name. Behind this gate, HTTP Basic is the gate's, and the app does not hear it: Too many wrong guesses from one address, or from anywhere at one environment, make the next ones wait. So that nobody else's guesses keep you out for long, a password that was right lately needs no check, and those already in are not affected. Signing in A browser goes to the console to sign in, and comes back. Whoever has a role in the app's project gets through; --any-user lets in anyone with an account. Being let in lasts 12 hours. Losing an account or a role ends it within a minute, and so does signing out of the console or ending that session there, even for a stream or a WebSocket that is already open. The app hears who they are from these, which Moorage alone can send through itself, since anything a client sends by those names is removed, however they are spelled: Header X-Moorage-User The user's ID, which stays the same if their address changes X-Moorage-User-Email Their email address X-Moorage-User-Name Their name, if they have one A script sends an API token that has the gate scope, for a user who may get through, and the app does not hear of it: An Authorization header that is not a Moorage token is not for the gate, and stays for the app. A Moorage token never reaches an app, behind any gate, since it would let the app act as whoever sent it. Should the app believe them? Behind Moorage, on a machine it shares with nothing that might lie to it, it can. But instances listen on this machine's loopback, so that another app here can reach them directly, past the gate, and say what it likes. Where apps here do not trust one another, an app should check that a request came through Moorage: X-Moorage-Proxy-Token is the same as $MOORAGE_PROXY_TOKEN, which differs by environment. Apps that are not in containers all run as one user today, and can read each other's environment, so that the token only keeps out what runs apart from them. Giving each app a user of its own comes in a later release. Share links A link lets whoever holds it through any gate, without an account or a password: It is shown only when it is made, since only a hash of it is kept. It lasts a week unless you say otherwise, and up to a year. Opening it sets a cookie for that hostname, and goes on to the app. A link with a limited number of uses asks for a click, so that what fetches addresses to preview them, as chat programs do, does not use it up. Revoking one ends it, and within a minute the way in of everyone it let in. Someone already in stays who they are if they open a link. Only from some addresses A list of addresses goes with any gate. Anyone else is turned away, with no form and no link that helps: The list stays until it is replaced, or --anywhere takes it away. Behind a proxy, the address is the nearest one in X-Forwarded-For that is not a proxy listed as trusted: what a client said before that proves nothing. Anything on this machine can reach a server that trusts 127.0.0.1 as a proxy, and say what it likes, so that a list is no protection from other apps here. What else to know Cookies are each for one hostname and environment, and signed, and the app does not hear of them: others it sets are its own affair. Without HTTPS, an app on another hostname of this server can set cookies for this one, so that gates are for keeping out those who are not trying very hard: use HTTPS. Caches: what a gate guards is sent as private, so that a shared cache does not hand it to others. Search engines are asked to leave alone everything but production, whatever its gate. Those turned away do not wake an environment that is asleep, and do not count as using it. Cross-origin requests to a gated app from another site are turned away, since browsers send no cookies with a preflight. /.moorage/ on an app's hostname belongs to Moorage.

h: With no wildcard DNS: path routing
b: An environment is at its own hostname under the server's domain, such as shop.apps.example.com. It can also be at a hostname of your own, or a path on one, so that several apps can share a hostname. A hostname of your own, and what it needs. DNS A domain serves nothing until its DNS is seen to point here, by either of: a CNAME to the environment's own hostname, which moor domains and the app's Domains and access tab show you, or an A or AAAA record with an address of this server. Moorage looks when it is attached, then every few minutes, or when you ask: A domain goes with one environment, and takes --env like everything else. Attaching one takes a maintainer. A hostname under the server's own domain is not needed: it names its apps by itself. Certificates With tls.mode = "acme", a domain gets a certificate of its own the first time it is asked for, once its DNS points here. The CA that Moorage makes for itself vouches only for the server's own domain, so that otherwise, HTTPS at another hostname needs one of these: [tls] mode = "files" with a certificate for that hostname, or a proxy in front that has one. A path on a hostname Requests under the path go to the environment, and the longest path that fits wins. What an app must know of it: It hears the path as it was asked for, and X-Forwarded-Prefix says what the path is. Most frameworks have a "root path" or "base" setting for this. --strip-prefix takes it away instead. Its redirects and cookies are made to fit. A Location: /login becomes /reports/login, and a cookie's path goes under /reports/. What is in what it sends is its own affair. Links in its pages are not rewritten: that goes wrong in ways nobody can see. Relative links always work; others need to take the path into account. Static sites work as long as their links are relative. /.moorage/ under the path belongs to Moorage. Prefer a hostname of its own for an app, if you can have one: it is the only way it can be sure of having cookies and storage to itself. With no wildcard DNS: path routing If you cannot have a wildcard DNS record, a whole server can give every app a path on one hostname, and /shop/, /docs/ and /shop--staging/ take the place of hostnames: That needs two DNS records, and no wildcard. The console must have a hostname of its own, and the server refuses to start without one: a page of any app on the console's own hostname could act as whoever is signed in. Each app hears its path, in $MOORAGE_BASE_PATH and X-Forwarded-Prefix, and $MOORAGE_URL says all of its address. strip_prefix = true in [app] takes it away from what it hears. Apps share one origin. A script in one page can read what another app's pages can, and cookies and browser storage are not kept apart. Use it where apps trust one another. Otherwise use hostnames: that is why they are the default.

Moorage is one program, moor: the server and the command line that talks to it. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, on amd64 and arm64. How big a machine says how much it needs. It needs no database, proxy or container engine. Builds download the Go, Node.js, uv and Python that an app asks for, from their official places or mirrors of your own. Beyond that: Git, on the machines that you push from, to deploy with git push. moor deploy does without it. Podman or Docker, on a server that runs apps in containers or services, such as a database. Nothing else asks for one, and a server with none says so when something does. systemd, on Linux, to run it as a service. macOS and Windows have what that takes. 1. Get moor On macOS or Linux: In PowerShell on Windows 11: Each picks the file for your computer from the latest release and downloads it with the release's SHA256SUMS. It requires exactly one matching checksum, runs the downloaded program's version check, and only then puts it in place, so a failed download never replaces a working copy. It needs no administrator rights, and starts nothing. Installs to PATH macOS, Linux ~/.local/bin/moor Left alone: it says what to add, if it is not there macOS, Linux, as root /usr/local/bin/moor Left alone Windows %LocalAppData%\Programs\Moorage\moor.exe Added to your user PATH: open a new terminal to use it For a server that will run as a system service, install as root, so that the service does not run from someone's home directory. Download and read the script first; never pipe a download straight into sudo: To choose a release or a directory, set these (MOOR_NO_PATH_UPDATE and MOOR_ARCH are for Windows only): Variable install.sh install.ps1 MOOR_VERSION --version -Version A release, such as v0.10.1. By default, the latest MOOR_INSTALL_DIR --install-dir -InstallDir An absolute directory MOOR_REPOSITORY -Repository owner/repository, for a fork MOOR_ARCH -Architecture amd64 or arm64, if detecting it fails MOOR_NO_PATH_UPDATE -NoPathUpdate Leave the user PATH alone On Windows, irm … | iex reads the script into memory and runs it, so the PowerShell execution policy, which governs script files, does not apply. To read it first, or for a saved copy: By hand Download the file for your system from the releases page, check it against SHA256SUMS, and put it on your PATH: (On Linux on ARM, use moor-linux-arm64. On macOS, use moor-darwin-arm64 or moor-darwin-amd64, and shasum -a 256 --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS. On Windows, use moor-windows-amd64.exe or moor-windows-arm64.exe, compare Get-FileHash with SHA256SUMS, and name it moor.exe, in a directory on your PATH.) The checksum shows a damaged download, and a file that differs from the release's list. Both come from the same release, so it cannot protect against someone able to replace both. Moorage's programs are not signed with an Apple or Microsoft certificate. The commands above download without a browser, so the system does not flag the file. If you save it with a browser, macOS or Windows SmartScreen asks for confirmation the first time it runs: on macOS, remove the flag with xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./moor-darwin-arm64, and on Windows, with Unblock-File .\moor-windows-amd64.exe. From source Build it with Go 1.26 or newer: moor version prints the version you have. 2. Configure the server moor server init writes server.toml, the server's configuration, from a preset. Run it as root for a server that starts with the machine (the file goes to /etc/moorage/server.toml on Linux, /Library/Application Support/Moorage/server.toml on macOS), in an elevated terminal on Windows for the same (%ProgramData%\Moorage\server.toml), or as yourself to try Moorage on your own computer: everything then goes in one folder, ~/.moorage, on macOS and Linux, and in %LocalAppData%\Moorage on Windows. XDG_CONFIG_HOME and XDG_DATA_HOME win on Linux, if they are set. A server set up as yourself by an earlier version stays where it is, and moor finds it. To move one, stop it, move the folder, change data_dir in server.toml, and start it again. A service names where its server.toml was, so that one takes moor server install from the new place. On your own computer — apps at http://<app>.localhost:8080: Chromium- and Firefox-based browsers resolve *.localhost names on their own. Where the rest of your computer does not, for Safari and command-line tools, moor server resolver install sets that up. Or, for curl and other tools, send the app's name as the Host header (curl -H 'Host: hello.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8080/). A server on your network — apps at https://<app>.<domain>, with certificates from Moorage's own certificate authority: Point a wildcard DNS record, *.apps.example.com, at the server, and open ports 80, 443 and 2222. With no wildcard record to be had, --routing path puts apps at <domain>/<app>. Browsers trust the certificates once they trust Moorage's CA, which every app serves at /.moorage/ca.crt, and moor trust installs (TLS and trusting the server). To use your own certificates — a corporate wildcard, for instance — set tls.mode = "files" and list them under [[tls.certificates]]; an intermediate CA from your corporate CA can issue certificates instead (tls.ca_cert, tls.ca_key). A server on the internet — apps at https://<app>.<domain>, with certificates from a public CA, and everything but production behind a sign-in: Point a wildcard DNS record at the server, and open ports 80, 443 and 2222. See From a public CA, with ACME, and read Security first: Moorage has not yet had an outside security review. Behind a TLS proxy such as nginx — Moorage serves plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1:8080 and your proxy terminates TLS: The proxy must keep the Host header, pass WebSocket upgrades, not buffer responses, and allow long requests and large uploads. moor server proxy-config nginx writes a configuration for nginx: see Behind a TLS proxy. Every setting is explained in the file itself; moor server run checks it strictly and name

Moorage itself asks for little: about 100 MB of memory, and next to no CPU while nothing is happening. What a machine has to hold is your apps, and only those awake. An environment asleep uses no memory until a request wakes it. We check this with a script on a machine limited to 4 CPUs and 8 GB: 60 environments of 10 apps, each a small Python server holding 64 MB, with sleep on. With 60 environments Measured Memory, all awake 4.9 GB Memory, all asleep 120 MB The server's own memory, at its most 107 MB The server's CPU, all asleep under 1% of a core Waking one with a request 0.13 s for this app: yours takes as long as it takes to start Waking all 60 at once 2.3 s for the slowest Serving five while the others sleep 4,100 requests a second, 95% within 12 ms Requests that failed none So count what your apps use while they are awake, and how many of them will be at once. Builds need room as well, which depends on what you build, and logs and metrics take disk.

h: What a release can be checked against
b: Back up That holds the database, repositories, builds, apps' data, certificates and a dump of each service of production and the named environments, and the server goes on running. Keep keys/master.key safe, and apart from your backups: it encrypts the apps' secrets, and a backup leaves it out. See backups for a schedule, buckets and restoring. Upgrading From 0.6.0, a server upgrades itself. To get to 0.6.0 from an earlier version, run the installer once, and restart the server. Before you do: Read what will be different. The changelog has a list of things to know under each release. Read the list of each one that you are crossing, and you need not stop at any of them: CI upgrades from the last release and from 0.6.0, with apps running. Start the server, if it has stopped, with moor server start. moor server status says. An upgrade only goes back by itself if the server was running, as there is otherwise nothing to restart: it replaces the binary, and nothing is watching when you start it. Make a backup, if what it holds matters. An upgrade keeps a copy of the database, for going back, and no more than that. Leave out the sudo if you installed the service without it, as the service is then your own. Use the moor that the service runs: moor server upgrade says so if this is another. That downloads the newest release and checks it against the checksum published with it. It then keeps a copy of the database, in upgrades in the data directory, and of the binary, as moor.previous beside it, puts the new binary in place, and restarts the server. Running apps keep running, and the new server takes them over. If the server does not come up on the new version, everything goes back by itself. A database from a large server can take a while to migrate: --wait 10m gives it longer than the 2 minutes it otherwise has. Option What it does --check Only says whether there is a newer version --version 0.6.1 Upgrades to that version, and not the newest --from DIR Takes the release from a directory or an address, for a mirror or a machine with no way out. It holds a release's files --wait 10m Gives the new version longer to come up To go back later: That puts back the binary, and leaves the database alone if the new version did not change it. If it did, the previous version could not read it, so it goes back to its copy from before the upgrade. What has happened since is then lost from it, so after 10 minutes this takes --force, and what it replaced is kept beside the copy, in upgrades in the data directory. There is one way back: from the last upgrade. A server that nothing manages, run with moor server run, gets its new binary, and goes on with the version it started with until you restart it. To go back, stop it first. To see that all is well afterwards, with sudo for a system service: Upgrade moor on the other machines that use the server too, by running the installer again: a newer server may change what the API answers. A server from before 0.1.0 has no accounts yet: moor server status shows the link to create the first, and until then the admin token works from anywhere, as it did. With the installer The installer can upgrade a server as well, without the copies or the way back. Run it again as the same user, which replaces moor where it is and says what it upgraded from, and restart the server: Until you do, a server goes on with the version it started with. A newer server changes the database as it starts, after keeping a copy in backups in the data directory, and an older one refuses a database that has moved on. So to go back to an earlier version in this way: stop the server, put that copy in the place of moorage.db, and give the installer the version with MOOR_VERSION. moor server upgrade --rollback only goes back from the version it upgraded to, and says so if the installer has been at work since. On Windows, the server and the supervisors of its apps run from moor.exe, and a running program cannot be replaced there, so both ways move it aside, where it goes on running. A server run in a terminal needs Ctrl+C and starting again. What a release can be checked against Each release has SHA256SUMS, a list of what went into the binaries in moorage-sbom.cdx.json, and an attestation of the workflow that built them. An upgrade and the installer both check a download against SHA256SUMS, which comes from the same place over HTTPS. That catches a damaged download, and a change on the way, and would not catch someone who could change the release itself. The attestation is GitHub's own record of what its build made, and that you can look at yourself: Uninstalling First, if your apps have services: what they hold is in volumes in the container engine, and uninstalling the server leaves those there. While the server still runs, deleting an app takes its services with it, and moor services remove takes one on its own: If you have already gone further than that, your engine still lists them, and podman volume rm takes one. This is for Podman, and Docker takes the same: If you changed what a computer trusts or resolves, take that back, on each one where you did: Then stop the server, its apps and their services, and remove the service: Then delete the program: ~/.local/bin/moor or /usr/local/bin/moor, with moor.previous beside it if it has upgraded itself. On Windows, that is the %LocalAppData%\Programs\Moorage folder, whose entry you can also remove from your user PATH (Settings → System → About → Advanced system settings → Environment Variables), and the %ProgramFiles%\Moorage folder, where installing the service puts a copy. The configuration and the data stay. Delete server.toml, which moor server status names, and the data directory that it names under data_dir, only if you no longer need the apps' data and the keys in it. A server set up as yourself has both in one folder, ~/.moorage, or %LocalAppData%\Moorage on Windows. What moor itself remembers of the servers it signs in to is in config.toml in ~/.moo

server.toml holds what the server needs before it can open its database. moor server init writes it, with a comment for each setting. Change the file and restart the server to apply it. A mistake stops the server, and says which setting, with the line for a syntax error or a setting it does not know, so that a typing error is not quietly ignored. Everything else is kept in the database, and changed in the console or with moor: see Settings in the database. Where it is As root, or an elevated Administrator As yourself Linux /etc/moorage/server.toml ~/.moorage/server.toml macOS /Library/Application Support/Moorage/server.toml ~/.moorage/server.toml Windows %ProgramData%\Moorage\server.toml %LocalAppData%\Moorage\server.toml --config or $MOORAGE_CONFIG names another. moor server status says which one a server uses. These variables override what the file says: Variable Overrides MOORAGE_DATA_DIR data_dir MOORAGE_LOG_LEVEL [log] level MOORAGE_LOG_FORMAT [log] format Presets local lan lan --behind-proxy public For This computer A server on your network A server behind nginx or the like A server on the internet Apps at http://<app>.localhost:8080 https://<app>.<domain> https://<app>.<domain> https://<app>.<domain> listen.http 127.0.0.1:8080 :80 127.0.0.1:8080 :80 listen.https :443 :443 listen.ssh 127.0.0.1:2222 :2222 :2222 :2222 tls.mode off internal off acme tls.hsts true access.named, access.preview public, login public, login public, login login, login proxy.trusted 127.0.0.1, ::1 proxy.external_scheme http https https https An example The top level Setting Default What it says data_dir required Where the server keeps its database, builds, logs and apps' data. An absolute path. domain required Apps are at <app>.<domain>. Point a wildcard DNS record, *.<domain>, at the server. console_host moorage.<domain> The hostname of the console, the API and git over HTTPS. routing "host" host gives every app a hostname of its own. path puts apps under /<app>/ on the domain, for where there can be no wildcard record: see path routing. The console then needs a hostname of its own. [listen] Setting Default What it says http required Where it answers plain HTTP. With TLS, it redirects to HTTPS. https Where it answers HTTPS. Empty when Moorage does not terminate TLS. ssh Where git pushes arrive over SSH. Empty turns that off. dns A loopback address where it answers DNS for its domain, for moor server resolver. [tls] See TLS and trusting the server. Setting Default What it says mode "internal" with listen.https, otherwise "off" internal: certificates from Moorage's own CA, or from an intermediate of yours. files: certificates you provide. acme: certificates from a public CA or an internal ACME server. off: plain HTTP, such as behind a proxy. ca_cert, ca_key With internal, an intermediate CA issued by your company's, so that its certificates are already trusted. Without them, Moorage makes its own root. hsts false Tells browsers to use nothing but HTTPS for each hostname here: see Staying on HTTPS. [[tls.certificates]], once for each, with mode = "files": Setting What it says cert A certificate chain, in a PEM file key Its private key, in a PEM file [tls.acme], with mode = "acme": see From a public CA, with ACME. Setting Default What it says agree_terms required Must be true: it says that you have read and accept the CA's terms. directory Let's Encrypt The address of the ACME server's directory. email Whom the CA tells of what it has to say about the account. ca_file The root to trust an internal ACME server by. challenges both How a hostname is shown to be this server's: http-01, on port 80, and tls-alpn-01, on port 443. [tls.acme.dns], for one certificate for the whole domain: Setting What it says provider cloudflare, rfc2136 or command token_file With cloudflare, the file that holds its API token server With rfc2136, the DNS server, as host:port key_name, key_file, key_algorithm With rfc2136, its TSIG key: its name, the file that holds its base64 secret, and its algorithm, by default hmac-sha256 command With command, a program run as add NAME VALUE and remove NAME VALUE wait With command, how long to give a record to reach the CA. By default 30s resolvers With cloudflare or rfc2136, the DNS servers to look for the record through, as host:port. By default the system's [proxy] See Behind a TLS proxy. Setting Default What it says trusted none Addresses or prefixes of the proxies whose X-Forwarded-* headers and PROXY protocol are believed. external_scheme "https" with TLS or a trusted proxy, otherwise "http" The scheme browsers use to reach Moorage. [access] Who may reach each kind of environment, unless its manifest or a maintainer says otherwise. Each is public, password, login or share: see Who can reach an app. Setting Default production "public" named "public" preview "login" A manifest may ask for another gate, but it may not open an environment to public where this does not. [isolation] See How apps are kept apart. Setting Default What it says level "auto" auto is user where the server runs as root on Linux, and none elsewhere. user gives each app an operating system user of its own. sandbox also confines it to its own files, with Landlock. uid_base 300000 Where the users of apps start. [auth] For a proxy that signs people in. See How people sign in. Setting Default What it says trusted_header The header in which the proxy says who someone is. It counts only from proxy.trusted, which it needs. trusted_name_header The header with their name, if there is one. trusted_provision false Make an account for someone new, the first time the proxy says who they are. [notifications] See Notifications. Setting Default What it says allow none Addresses and prefixes that webhooks, mail servers, telemetry sinks and forges may be at, though they would be refused as this machine, a link-local address or a cloud's metadata service. disk_percent 90 How full the data volume may get before someone is told. [toolchains] Build

h: A checklist for a shared server
b: Moorage asks little of whoever runs it. This page says what to set up in the first week, what to look at after that, and what changes as a server grows. Installing Moorage comes first. The first week Check it. moor server doctor looks at the server and what it depends on, and says how to fix what it finds. Decide about TLS, if you have not. A public CA, or an intermediate from your company's, means nobody has to trust anything by hand. Keep apps apart. On a shared Linux server, run as root and use level = "user" or "sandbox" in [isolation]. moor server doctor and the System page say what you have. How apps are kept apart says what each gives you. Add people. Give most people a role in a project, and only a few the administrator's. Accounts and access says how, and How people sign in connects your identity provider. Back up. Set a schedule in Settings → Backups, and keep keys/master.key somewhere apart: without it, the secrets in a backup cannot be read, and with it, anyone can. Then try a restore. See Backups. Be told. Add a channel and a rule in Settings → Notifications, so that a failed deployment, a crash loop, a failed cron job, a full disk or a failed backup reaches someone. See Notifications. Close the ports you do not use. Moorage needs its HTTP and HTTPS ports, and the SSH port if you push over SSH. Apps are told to listen on loopback, and moor server doctor warns of one that can be reached another way. What to look at The console's Settings → System has what the server runs, and what the checks find: Settings → System: the same checks as moor server doctor. From the command line: Who did what is in the audit log, for a year: each change, sign-in, secret revealed and git push, with who and how it went, and where from for all but pushes. Settings → Audit log searches and downloads it, and moor audit shows it. Settings → Audit log. How it is doing is in metrics, for Prometheus as well as the console, and can go on to an OpenTelemetry collector. The server's health answers at /.moorage/health on every hostname, for whatever watches your machines. Where the disk goes Everything is under the data directory, in plain files you can look at: Folder What it holds What limits it moorage.db The database Grows slowly. Events go after 90 days, the audit log after a year repos Apps' git repositories The size of their history builds Builds, and uploads for redeploying keep_releases in each manifest: five by default data Apps' own data The apps. Moorage keeps nothing of its own here logs Apps', deployments' and the server's logs Rotation at 10 MiB, five files back, and 14 days for stopped instances. Deployments' logs stay until their app or environment goes toolchains, cache Toolchains and build caches One copy of each version, shared by every app backups Database copies before each migration, and backups if you send them there The last three migrations; your schedule's keep keys, certs The master key, SSH host keys and the CA Small. Back up keys apart moor server doctor looks at free space, and a server tells those concerned when the data volume passes disk_percent in [notifications], 90% by default. Deleting an app removes its builds, logs and repository, and its data unless you keep it. Previews remove themselves when their branch goes, or after seven days unused. As it grows Let environments sleep. An environment asleep uses no memory until a request wakes it, which is why a server can hold far more environments than it could run at once. How big a machine has what we measured. Limit what apps can use. [resources] in a manifest limits an instance's memory and CPU. They are enforced on Linux when the server runs as root with cgroup v2, and on Windows. Elsewhere, an instance over its memory limit is restarted. There is one machine. Moorage does not spread apps over several, and no version so far does. When a server is full, move some apps to another with a backup and a restore, or with their source. Stopping and restarting Apps do not depend on the server being up. Stopping, restarting or upgrading it leaves them running and serving what is in flight, and it takes them over again when it starts. To stop the apps and their services too, whether or not the server is running: When something is wrong has more on that. Upgrading It checks what it downloads, keeps a copy of the database and of the binary, and goes back by itself if the new version does not come up. See Upgrading. A checklist for a shared server Isolation at user or sandbox. Certificates from a public CA, an intermediate CA or files of your own, and not a root that everyone trusts by hand. The console on its own hostname, which is the default. Behind a proxy, the HTTP listener on loopback or a private address, and only the proxy's addresses in [proxy] trusted. Few administrators, and two-factor sign-in or single sign-on for them. Previews behind login, which is the default. keys/master.key backed up, and apart from your backups. A restore tried. A firewall in front of everything but the ports above. API tokens limited to one app and a scope, with an expiry, for each script. Security says what these protect against, and what they do not.

h: From a public CA, with ACME
One certificate for the whole domain
Another CA, or one of your own
b: Moorage serves apps over TLS in one of four ways, chosen by tls.mode in server.toml: tls.mode Certificates For internal Issued by Moorage's own CA, for each hostname as it is first asked for, and renewed by themselves A server on your network. The default files Files you provide under [[tls.certificates]], such as a corporate wildcard, reloaded when they change A company that issues its own acme From a public CA, or an internal ACME server, and renewed by themselves A server on the internet off None: plain HTTP Behind a TLS proxy, or on your own computer A certificate from the internal CA goes only to the console's hostname and to names of apps under the base domain, so a stranger's guess at a hostname gets nothing. Trusting the internal CA Browsers warn about the certificates of a CA they do not know. On each computer that uses the server, once: The CA goes into the operating system's list, which Safari, Chrome and Edge use on macOS and Windows, and command-line tools on Linux. On Linux it also goes into the lists Chromium and Firefox keep for themselves, if certutil is installed. Firefox may keep its own list on other systems too: moor trust --print writes the certificate, to import in its settings. The CA that Moorage generates may sign only for the server's domain, so trusting it does not let the server pretend to be your bank. moor trust says what a CA may sign for, and warns of one that may sign for any site. On the server's own machine moor trust reads the server's files, and asks nothing In a script moor trust --server URL --fingerprint AB:CD:… asks nothing if the fingerprint matches, and fails if it does not With a file you obtained safely moor trust --file corporate-root.pem To see it and change nothing moor trust --print To take it back moor trust --remove On macOS and Windows, moor trust changes your own list, and the system asks you to confirm; with sudo or as an Administrator, it changes the machine's. On Linux it uses sudo, which may ask for your password. On macOS, --remove may also ask someone at the screen to confirm removing the trust setting: after two minutes with no answer, the certificate is gone and the setting stays, and moor trust says so. The fingerprint is also in the server's log when it starts. Each server's CA is at /.moorage/ca.crt, for anyone who would rather install it by hand. moor itself uses the system's list. On a machine where you would rather not change it, --ca-cert FILE trusts a CA for one command, and moor login --ca-cert for one server. With your company's CA Company machines usually trust a company's root already. An intermediate CA issued from it, and ideally limited to the base domain, makes Moorage's certificates trusted everywhere with nothing to install: Or use a wildcard certificate for the base domain: moor server doctor checks the certificates: that they exist, match their keys, cover the hostnames, and when they expire. From a public CA, with ACME What this has been tried against. CI runs each way of getting a certificate described here against Pebble, the test server that Let's Encrypt publishes, and RFC 2136 against a real DNS server. It has not yet got a certificate from Let's Encrypt itself, or set a record at Cloudflare. If you try them first, please say how it goes. --agree-terms says that you have read and accept the terms of Let's Encrypt, which is the CA unless you say otherwise. Point a wildcard DNS record, *.apps.example.com, at the server, and open ports 80 and 443 to the internet, as that is where the CA looks. That is all: a certificate comes the first time a hostname is asked for, and is renewed by itself. Browsers already trust it, so there is nothing to install. The preset also puts everything but production behind a sign-in. See [access]. Only what the server serves gets a certificate: the console, and the hostnames of apps, environments and your own domains that it knows. A CA limits how many certificates a domain can have, and anyone who connects can say any name they like, so a made-up name gets nothing, and the CA is not asked. One certificate for the whole domain Each hostname having its own certificate is simple, but Let's Encrypt allows 50 for a domain each week, the first visit to each waits a few seconds for one, and each name is published in the CA's public logs. With many previews, get one certificate for *.apps.example.com instead, which takes showing the CA a DNS record, so tell Moorage how to set one: The file holds an API token that can edit that zone's DNS, and should be readable only by the server. The server gets the certificate when it starts. Your own domains, which are not under that wildcard, still get one each. For a DNS server of your own, rfc2136 sends it signed updates: For anything else, command runs a program of yours, which sets a TXT record on any DNS service you can reach from a script: It is run as moorage-dns add _acme-challenge.apps.example.com VALUE before the CA looks, and with remove afterwards. wait is how long to give the record to reach the servers the CA asks. A failure, and what the program said, goes in the server's log. Another CA, or one of your own directory names another ACME server, and ca_file the root to trust it by, if that is not a public one: To try it first, with no limits to speak of, use Let's Encrypt's staging directory, https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory, whose certificates browsers do not trust. When it cannot get one moor server doctor says how many certificates there are and when the next one ends. A certificate is renewed when a third of its life is left, and if that fails, the server's log says why, it goes on trying, and those concerned are told, once, and again when it has worked. What it was serving goes on being served until the certificate ends. Port 80 and port 443 are what a CA checks, on the hostname itself. With only one of them open, challenges = ["http-01"] or ["tls-alpn-01"] says which to use. Behind a port forward, or with

If you already run nginx or a load balancer for its certificates, its access logs or because policy asks for one, Moorage can serve plain HTTP behind it: Headers such as X-Forwarded-For are believed only from the addresses under trusted. From anywhere else they are ignored, so nobody can pretend to be someone else by sending them. X-Moorage-* headers from clients are always removed. nginx moor server proxy-config writes the configuration, for this server's hostnames: The certificate must cover the console's hostname and *.<domain>. CI runs a server behind a real nginx with this configuration, and deploys and pushes through it. Any other proxy Whatever stands in front of Moorage must: send the console's hostname and *.<domain> to Moorage, keeping the Host header: Moorage routes by it; set X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto; pass WebSocket upgrades on, with HTTP/1.1 and the Upgrade and Connection headers; not buffer responses, or logs and deploys will not show as they happen. Moorage marks these responses with X-Accel-Buffering: no; allow long requests: a git push over HTTPS stays open for its whole deployment, and a followed log can be silent for long. Limits of a minute break them; allow large requests: an upload or a push may be up to 1 GiB, and Moorage limits them itself. /.moorage/health answers on every hostname, for a load balancer's health checks. Check the whole path On the server's machine, with the address people use: --timeouts adds over a minute to the check, to catch a limit of a minute. --ca-cert names the issuer of the proxy's certificate, if the system does not trust it.

h: Sign in from the command line
b: Moorage has user accounts, API tokens and SSH keys. On your own computer you need none of them: the command line on the server's machine finds the server and its local admin token by itself. Accounts are for everyone else, and for every other machine. Claim the server moor server init prints a one-time setup link; moor server status and the server's log show it too, until it has been used: Open it and create the first account, which is the server's administrator. Only someone who can read the link can do this, so nobody can race you to a server that has just been installed. Sign in from the command line From any machine: Your browser opens the server's approval page. Sign in there, check that the code it shows is the one in your terminal, and approve: the command line receives a token, and no password is typed into the terminal. The server and token are saved as a context, in config.toml in your user's configuration directory ($MOOR_CONFIG overrides it), readable only by you. On a machine with no browser, open the address it prints on another machine, or create a token elsewhere and pass it on standard input: With Moorage's own CA, add --ca-cert ca.crt; the context remembers it. Add people An admin creates accounts, and sends each person a one-time link to choose a password. Moorage does not send email itself. Settings → Users. Command What it does moor server users Lists the users moor server users create EMAIL [--name N] [--admin] Creates a user, and prints their link moor server users invite EMAIL Prints a new link: for a forgotten password, or one that expired moor server users role EMAIL admin|member Changes a role moor server users disable EMAIL Ends their sessions; their tokens and keys stop working moor server users enable EMAIL Enables them again Passwords have at least 12 characters, and the most common ones are refused. Moorage keeps only an Argon2id hash. The last enabled admin cannot be demoted or disabled. Roles. An admin manages the server and its users, and may do everything with every app. What a member may do depends on their role in each project. Projects and roles Apps belong to projects, and people have roles in projects: A project's page. Viewer Deployer Maintainer Admin See the app, its status and its deployments ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Read its logs ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Deploy, restart, roll back and scale; see its variables and its manifest, but not secrets ✓ ✓ ✓ Change its variables, reveal secrets, move it; manage the project's members ✓ ✓ Make projects, manage users and the server; read the audit log ✓ Someone with no role in a project sees nothing of it. Its apps are in no list or feed, and the API, the console and git answer as they would for an app that is not there. It has two limits. An app's name is shared with the whole server, since it is a hostname, so that someone who tries to take a name finds out that it is taken. And an app's address answers whoever can reach the server, if only to say that there is a gate there. Every server starts with one project, default, in which everyone is a maintainer: nothing changes until you say so. So a team that trusts each other needs do nothing. To keep an app apart, make a project for it: moor projects set NAME --everyone viewer gives everyone else a role, and --everyone none takes it away, which you can do to default too. --viewers-see-logs=false keeps logs from viewers, because logs can hold what they should not see. That goes for what a failed deployment printed and the commands that people have run, too. A first deployment makes its app in default, which takes a role there. A token can do no more than its owner, and its scope can narrow that further: a token with the read scope only reads, whatever its owner's role. Deploying is running code on the server, so give deployer to people you would give shell access. Who did what Every change through the API or the console, every sign-in, every push and every secret revealed is kept for a year, with who, from where, what to, and how it went. Nothing of what was sent goes in the record. Administrators read it under Settings, Audit log: Settings → Audit log. The API has it at GET /api/v1/audit, and ?format=ndjson gives all of it, to keep. Two-factor sign-in Your account → Two-factor adds a code from an authenticator app to signing in with a password: scan what it shows, and enter the code the app makes to turn it on. You get ten recovery codes, once each, for if you lose the app. Keep them somewhere safe. A code or a recovery code works once. Someone who has lost both can have an administrator turn it off for them, in Settings → Users, and a link to choose a new password does not get round it. API tokens and SSH keys are separate from it, and signing in from moor login goes through your browser. API tokens Tokens are for scripts, CI, and git over HTTPS. A token can do what its scope allows and its owner may do. Your API tokens, under your account. The secret is printed to standard output, this once. Moorage keeps only its hash. Scope What it allows read See apps, deployments, releases, instances and logs; fetch repositories deploy Also deploy, restart, roll back and push; see variables admin Also change variables; manage its owner's tokens, keys and sessions; for an admin, manage users --app restricts a token to one app: it sees and reaches nothing else, and cannot manage credentials. --envs previews limits a read or deploy token to previews, for a coding agent. --expires ends it after a time. moor tokens lists yours with when each was last used, and moor tokens revoke NAME ends one at once. Scripts pass a token with MOOR_TOKEN (and MOOR_SERVER), or --token. SSH keys moor keys add registers your public key on your account, so that your pushes over SSH are yours (Deploying with git push). A key belongs to one account. Your SSH keys, under your account. The server's local admin token The server writes an admin token to keys/admin-token in its data directory, readable only by the server's user. It le

h: Behind a proxy that signs people in
b: Everyone starts with an email address and a password. Two-factor sign-in adds a code to that, and a server can leave signing in to your own identity provider, or to a proxy in front of it. Single sign-on Settings → Sign-in connects the server to any provider that speaks OpenID Connect. Tell the provider the address that page shows, which it sends people back to, and give the page: Its address. The server finds the rest there, and will not save until it has. It has to be https. A client ID and secret, from your provider. The secret is sealed with the master key. What the button says. The sign-in page then offers that button beside the password form. Try it in a private window before you sign out. Who gets in Someone with an account already joins up by their email address the first time, as long as the provider says that the address is verified. From then on they are who the provider says, whatever their address becomes. If your provider leaves that out, as some do, and nobody can choose their own address there, tick Take your provider's word. Otherwise, they are told to ask you. A provider that says an address is unverified is never believed. Someone with no account gets one the first time if you tick Make an account, as a member who can look at the default project and do nothing else, until a group or you say otherwise. Everyone else is a maintainer of that project unless you have changed it, under Projects. Say which addresses this is for with Addresses at, or anyone your provider signs in gets an account. What they may do Their groups can say. Ask your provider for them, usually with a scope and a claim that are both called groups, and say what they mean, one to a line: These are applied each time someone signs in: they get the highest role that their groups give in each project, and lose what they no longer have. What the rules do not mention stays as you set it, so that without a rule for admin, it stays yours to give by hand. A rule says that its group decides that project: someone not in the group has no more than a look at it, even in one that gives everyone more. If your provider says nothing of someone's groups, in its token or when asked for their user info, that counts as none, as some leave them out for someone in no groups, and the server's log says so: if they do have some, it may need a scope, or the claim's name. Whoever is the last administrator stays one. Only through your provider Only sign in through the provider turns off passwords, in the console and the API, and links to choose one. API tokens and SSH keys go on working, and so does moor login, which goes through your browser. Two-factor sign-in is then up to your provider. If your provider goes away, on the server's own machine: That turns single sign-on off and gives passwords back. Someone who only ever signed in through the provider has no password, and moor server users invite EMAIL prints a link to choose one. Two-factor sign-in See accounts. It applies to signing in with a password, and is up to your provider for someone who signs in through one. Under your account. Behind a proxy that signs people in If something in front of Moorage already signs people in, such as an authenticating proxy, it can say who they are in a header: The header counts only from the addresses under [proxy] trusted, and your proxy has to replace any copy of it that a client sends. Otherwise anyone could say that they are anyone. The server refuses to start with a trusted_header and no trusted proxy, and it is best if nothing else can reach it at all (Behind a TLS proxy says how). Claim the server first, with its setup link, which works through the proxy: until there is an administrator, the header is ignored, so that the first person to come by does not make the server theirs. Someone who gets an account from trusted_provision can look at the default project and do nothing else until you say. Run that proxy on another machine. Apps deployed on this server can reach it from any of this machine's addresses, so if a trusted range holds one of those, an app could say that it is anyone. The server warns about this when it starts. If you can only run them together, use this for a server whose apps you trust as you trust your administrators. Signing out of Moorage signs them in again at once, as the proxy still says who they are: signing out is up to the proxy. The API goes on asking for a token. See also Accounts and access Who can reach an app: the same sign-in can guard your apps

h: With a user of its own
b: On a server that several people deploy to, one app should not be able to read another's data or secrets, or take all of its memory. How far Moorage can see to that depends on the system, and it tells you what is in effect: on an app's page in the console, in Settings → System, and from moor server doctor. The levels Level What it does Where none Every app runs as the same user as the server, and can read what the others can, and what the server can: its database and master key. Everywhere user Each app runs as an operating system user of its own, and its builds as another. Linux, with the server running as root sandbox As user, and each app can only read its own build, toolchains and system files, can only write to its own data and temporary directories, and can only listen on its own port. Linux 5.13 or newer, with the server running as root server.toml says which: Without that, it is auto: user where the server runs as root on Linux, as the system service does, and none elsewhere. Asking for a level that this system cannot have stops the server from starting, with the reason. auto settles for what it can get, and says why. This is a server-wide setting: a change takes effect for each instance as it next starts, so restart your apps after changing it. Moorage assumes that those who deploy are teammates and not adversaries. Isolation prevents accidents and limits the damage if one app is broken into. It does not make a server safe for strangers' code, which needs virtual machines. With a user of its own An app's users come from a range that starts at 300000, or at uid_base under [isolation]. They need no entries in /etc/passwd, and an app keeps its user for good, so that uid_base is to be set before there are apps: a server refuses to run one as a user below it. Its data directory belongs to it, and no other app can enter it. Its build is read-only. Other apps cannot read its environment, including its secrets, from /proc. moor run, cron jobs and release commands run as the app's user. Builds run as a user of their own in the app's group, with a cache of their own, so that what a package's install script does cannot reach the app's data or another app's builds. An app can only write to $MOORAGE_DATA_DIR and $TMPDIR. One that writes beside its own code has to change, since its build is read-only. Upgrading a server that already runs as root changes who its apps run as when they next start, and Moorage gives them their data directories then. Instances that were running through the upgrade go on as root until they restart, which the app's page and Settings → System say: moor restart APP does it without downtime, and the other apps cannot read their files in the meantime. An app that reads something only root can read will stop being able to, and level = "none" keeps it as it was while you look into that. Coming back from none, an app gets back what it wrote as root the next time it starts. An app's environments share its user, so that a preview can read production's data and variables. Keep what should not meet in apps of their own. /dev/shm is left writable in a sandbox too, as programs expect it to be, and is shared between apps, under the usual file permissions. An environment's data can be a link to a bigger disk, in data/<app>: the app's user gets what it leads to, and a backup holds that, so that a restore brings it back as a plain directory. The data directory and moor itself have to be where other users can reach them. /var/lib/moorage and /usr/local/bin, where the system service puts them, are. If they are not, auto stays at none and says so. In a sandbox Besides what user does, it sets no_new_privs, so that nothing it runs can gain privileges, and uses Landlock to confine it. A kernel with an earlier version of Landlock restricts what it can: the limit on ports takes Linux 6.7. A kernel with none runs apps at the user level, and says so. Some programs expect more. One that writes to /tmp by its full name, rather than to $TMPDIR, fails in a sandbox, as does one that listens on a second port. On Windows There is one level there, none. The server runs as the account of its own that the service has, NT SERVICE\Moorage, and all apps run as it too, so that they are kept from the rest of the computer, and not from one another. Each instance runs in a Job Object, which holds it and all it starts to its limits, and ends them all together. They are not kept from the server either. An app can read what the account can, and that is the database and the master key, so it can read every app's secrets, and could change the server's configuration. On Windows, then, anyone who can deploy to this server can reach everything on it, whichever project they are in. Only let people deploy here if that is all right, or use Linux, where each app has a user of its own. The service keeps only the one privilege that it needs, so that an app cannot impersonate whoever connects to it. Its data directory is closed to everyone but the account, the system and administrators, which is why it has to be a folder of its own, and moor server install will not do that to the top of a drive or to anyone's profile. Limits [resources] in the manifest says how much each instance may use: Where Memory CPU and processes Linux, with the server running as root The kernel kills an instance over it, and the whole instance goes together. It cannot swap instead Enforced by the kernel Windows A Job Object holds each instance: what it asks for beyond its memory is refused, and it is not killed for that Enforced, by the same Job Object Anywhere else Moorage restarts an instance that stays over it for three samples, 30 seconds or so Not enforced, which the app's page says In a container The engine enforces it The engine enforces it An instance the kernel kills for its memory is restarted, and says so where it says how it last exited: out of memory. A command or cron job killed in that way fails, and says so too. One that Moorage restar

A backup holds what a server cannot make again: its database, the apps' repositories and builds, their data directories and the server's certificates. It is one file, and the server goes on running while it is made. Logs and caches are left out, and so are toolchains, which the server fetches again as the apps that need them start. Restored on a machine with no way out, those apps need a mirror, under [toolchains] in server.toml. Settings → Backups. Backups run where the server is, as the user that runs it, so that on a system service that takes sudo. The master key A backup leaves out keys/master.key, which encrypts the apps' secrets, so that a backup that goes astray gives them away to nobody. Without that key a backup's secrets are lost for good, so that keep it safe, and somewhere other than your backups. Restoring needs that key to be in place, and refuses before reading any further if it is not the one that the backup was made with. --include-keys puts the key and the server's other keys in the backup, for a directory that you keep as safe as they are. A bucket is refused: there, one wrong setting gives away every secret you have. A schedule Settings → Backups in the console says where they go, and how often: Where: a directory, or a bucket on S3 or a service like it. The secret key is sealed with the master key. Schedule: a cron expression, such as @daily or 0 3 * * *, in the server's time zone. One that was due while the server was down is made when it comes back. How many to keep: when a scheduled one finishes, older ones go. With nothing said, they go to backups/archives in the data directory. That is a start and not a plan, since whatever takes that disk takes them too. A backup that fails tells administrators in the console, and a channel with a rule for backup.failed. So does the next one that works. To a bucket From the command line, the service's details come from the usual variables: For a service other than AWS, AWS_ENDPOINT_URL says where it is, and buckets are then addressed by path. Temporary credentials need AWS_SESSION_TOKEN as well. Its parts go up as they are made, so that a backup needs neither memory nor disk for the whole of it, up to the 160 GB that its parts come to, and a part that fails is tried again. Without a --to, the command uses what Settings → Backups says. See what is there Read one through to see that it could be restored, without changing anything: Restoring Install the same version of Moorage or a newer one, configure it as before, and put the master key in place. Then, with the server stopped: It reads all of the backup to one side first, so that a damaged one changes nothing, and refuses one that did not finish or that does not hash to what was noted when it was made. On a server that already has a database, --force moves what is there aside rather than deleting it. Any apps still running are stopped just before the swap. The server starts them again when it starts, and brings an older backup's database up to date. Everyone can sign in as before, and browsers that trusted the server's own CA still do, as its key comes back, sealed in the backup with the master key. Restore to a data directory at the same path as before: builds can hold links to their toolchains by their full paths. Without --include-keys, the server has a new SSH host key, so that those who push over SSH are told that it has changed. Restore only your own backups. What a server restores, it goes on to run, and it refuses what no backup should hold, such as keys in one that says it has none. A .sha256 beside a backup shows that it is whole, and not who made it, so that whoever can write to where your backups go can change them: keep that as closed as the server. Apps with databases Services are looked after: a backup holds a dump of each, made just before. The data directories are read while the apps go on running, so that a file being written at that moment may be caught halfway. For most files that does not matter, but a database file copied while it is in use may not open again, and the command says how many files changed as they were read: the server's log does for those it makes itself. If an app keeps a database in its data directory, have a cron job dump it there shortly before the backup, and restore from the dump. For SQLite: The server's configuration A backup holds everything, to bring a server back. Its settings alone are a smaller thing, and a file you can read, keep with the rest of what you look after, or bring to another server: people and their roles, projects and who is in them, container registries, notification channels and rules, where backups go, and sign-in. Settings → System has the same file to download. It holds no secrets. Where one belongs, it names a variable of the environment: To bring it in, look first at what that would do: Then do it, with those secrets in the command's environment: It adds and changes, and removes nothing. What the file does not mention stays as it is, down to a single setting, and a server keeps the secret it has when the variable is not set, so that bringing a file back to the server it came from changes nothing. Only variables whose names start with MOORAGE_ are read: a file from someone else cannot ask for anything else in your environment. Something that cannot be done is said, and does not stop the rest; the command then fails. A dry run says the same, except that your identity provider is only asked when it is done. People's passwords and second factors do not go with them, so someone new needs moor server users invite, or single sign-on. A name only counts when it makes the account, and a disabled user stays disabled until you enable them. server.toml is apart from this: it is a file already, and is for you to copy. So are your apps: those come from their manifests and repositories, and a rule for an app that is not deployed yet is said to have failed, until it is. See also Installing Moorage Notifications

What this has been tried against. CI sends logs and metrics to a real OpenTelemetry collector, and logs to syslog-ng over UDP, TCP and TLS, on each change to this code. It has not met a hosted service. If yours disagrees, please say how it goes. Moorage keeps what apps say, in its logs, and what they do, in its metrics. It can send them somewhere else as well, if that is where your team looks, and tell you when an environment crosses a threshold. Sinks A sink is somewhere to send things, and it takes an administrator to add one. In the console, it is Settings, then Telemetry. From the command line: Settings → Telemetry. Kind Address Sends syslog udp://host:514, tcp://host:601 or tls://host:6514 Logs, as RFC 5424 otlp What comes before /v1/logs, as in https://otel.example.com:4318 Logs and metrics, as OTLP over HTTP, in JSON http Where to send it Logs, as JSON batches A sink sends all apps unless --app says which. Saving one with the same name changes it. It starts from about now: what was said before is not sent. Headers are kept sealed, and are not shown again. Saving a sink without them keeps those it has, unless its address has changed. They are not sent in the clear across the internet, so they take an https address, or one on the local network. A sink is held to what notifications may reach, and goes by [notifications] allow. What goes where What is sent is what is in the logs: what each instance says, and what each one-off command and cron job says, with secrets already taken out. What is said at a terminal is not kept, so it is not sent. Build logs and Moorage's own stay here. Syslog has a facility of local0, a severity of informational for standard output and error for standard error, the server's name as its host, the app's as its app name, the instance as its process ID, and the environment as its message ID. Over TCP and TLS each message has its length in front of it, as RFC 6587 has it. Over UDP, anything past 1,400 bytes is cut off. OTLP has a resource for each instance, with service.name as the app, deployment.environment.name, service.instance.id, moorage.process and host.name, and each record has log.iostream, of stdout, stderr or moorage. Moorage does not guess at a severity from what a line says. HTTP posts this, with up to 500 lines: stream is O for standard output, E for standard error, and M for a note from Moorage, such as that an instance restarted. Metrics go once a minute to an OTLP sink, with the same in them as /metrics has for a scrape, under names such as moorage.http.requests, moorage.http.request.duration, moorage.instance.cpu and moorage.host.disk.used. Counts are cumulative, from when the server started. --app has no effect on them. When a sink is down Nothing here waits for a sink. Each has a queue of 20,000 lines, and past that the oldest go, with a count of how many did. It tries again after a second, then two, and so on, to once a minute, and when it gets through it catches up. A sink that answers that it will not take what it was sent (400, 413 or 422) gets less at a time, and a single line that it will not take is let go of and counted, so that it does not stop what comes after. How that is going is in the console and in moor server telemetry. Apps go on through a restart of the server, and it catches up then too, from what is in the log files. What was in a queue as the server stopped is lost, so it is at most a few seconds' worth when all is well. This is for following what is going on. It is not a guarantee that each line gets there, and the record is the logs here. Thresholds A threshold says when to be told about how an environment is doing. On an app's Metrics tab, or: Metric What it compares In error-rate Answers that are 5xx, over the last minute Percent latency-p95 How long the slowest 5 requests in 100 took at least, over the last minute Milliseconds memory The instance using the most, against its [resources] limit Percent of the limit cpu The instance using the most Percent of one core Past one for as long as it says, the default being five minutes, a notification goes to whoever a rule sends A threshold is crossed to, and another goes when it comes right. A minute that has nothing to say counts for neither: an app no one is asking has no error rate, fewer than 5 requests is too few to call one, and memory has nothing to compare if there is no limit. It takes a maintainer of the app's project to add or remove one, and they belong to an environment. New rules ask for A threshold is crossed unless told otherwise, and rules from before do not, so that they go on doing what they did. The server's disk The server tells of its data volume at 90% full. To have it say sooner, or later, set this in server.toml and restart the server:

h: A build cannot get its toolchain
b: Ask the doctor Settings → System: the same checks, in the console. It checks a server on this machine, running or not, and says how to fix what it finds. Run it with sudo if the server runs as root, so that it can read the server's files. Check What it looks at server That it answers, is healthy, and is the version of this moor listen.* That it answers on each address; while it is stopped, that it could listen there dns The console's hostname and a made-up app's, through the system's resolver tls The CA or certificate files: that they exist, match, cover the hostnames, and how long they have left. Plain HTTP where it should not be containers That the engine is there and answers: a problem if server.toml names it, a warning if it was only found on this machine data, keys The data directory, and that nobody else can read its keys disk Free space where the data is clock That the clock is synchronised (Linux) kernel cgroup v2 and Landlock (Linux), which isolating native apps will use apps That no instance listens beyond loopback, where it could be reached without the router --public-url adds the path through a proxy. The exit status is 1 if anything failed, and --json prints the checks for a script. A build cannot get its toolchain A build downloads the toolchain it needs, and refuses one that does not match what the project publishes. "is signed by a key that this moor does not know". Node.js releases are signed by those who make them, whose keys come with moor. A new releaser's first release can come before the moor that knows them, so upgrade moor (upgrading) and deploy again. If you cannot yet, and have a mirror that leaves signatures out or trust the download for now, this goes on and says so in the build's log: "failed verification". What arrived is not what was published: its checksum or its signature is wrong, and signatures does not change that. A proxy may be changing it on the way, or a mirror may be damaged. Stopping everything Apps and services keep running when the server stops, on purpose. moor server stop stops the server, as a service or as started with moor server run; with --all it stops the apps too, in containers or not, and their services, whether or not a server is running: The server starts them again when it next starts. A service keeps what it holds. *.localhost does not resolve On your own computer, apps are at http://<app>.localhost:8080. Chromium- and Firefox-based browsers and systemd-resolved on Linux resolve those names by themselves, as do some versions of macOS. On the others, Safari and command-line tools do not, and this fixes that: It adds /etc/resolver/localhost, for which it uses sudo, and turns on a small DNS responder in the server, which answers on loopback only, for that domain only. Restart the server to take it up. moor server resolver shows where things stand, and moor server resolver remove undoes it. On Windows, it takes an elevated terminal, and adds a block with the names of what is deployed to the hosts file, which has no way of saying all of them at once. A server in an elevated terminal keeps it up to date, and otherwise, run it again after adding an app. Or send the name as the Host header: What happened moor events shows what happened on the server, and so does Activity in the console: deployments, releases, changes of variables, and instances that exited or sickened. Where the logs are Log The server's logs/server/moorage.log in the data directory, and the journal on Linux (journalctl -u moorage.service -f) An app's moor logs -f A deployment's moor deployments show ID Requests to an app logs/router/<app>/<env>.log in the data directory

moorage.toml, at the top of an app's directory, says how Moorage builds and runs the app. It is optional: without it, Moorage detects the kind of app (see Detection), and moor manifest explain shows what it detected. This page describes the manifest as Moorage 0.10.1 implements it; the design describes what later releases add. Rules Every key is optional, and an unknown key is an error, so that a typo fails at once. Tables whose names start with x- are left for other tools. Durations are strings such as "500ms", "90s", "10m" or "2h". Commands run in Moorage's embedded POSIX shell, the same on every operating system: &&, $VAR, quotes and redirections work everywhere. The programs a command calls must exist on the server. Secrets never go in the manifest. moor manifest validate warns about values that look like credentials; set them on the server with moor env set --secret (see Variables and secrets). An example [app] Key Default Description name — The app's name, used when moor deploy is not given --app: 3 to 40 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter. It is also the first part of the app's hostname. runtime "auto" auto (detect), go, python, node, static, command (your own build), binary (run the files as they are), or dockerfile or image (run in a container). toolchains [] More toolchains on the PATH while building and running, as name@version: go, node, python and uv are installed by Moorage, and name@system uses the server's own ("java@system"). Versions may be partial ("24", "3.13"); the exact version is recorded in the build. watch lists the paths that matter, as globs, whose * crosses slashes: a push that touches none of them, nor this file, is kept and not deployed. strip_prefix, with path routing, takes the path the app is served at away from what it hears. [go] Key Default Description version the toolchain line of go.mod, or else the newest patch release of its go line The Go that builds the app. Builds run with GOTOOLCHAIN=local. main . when it is package main, or else the single ./cmd/* The main package. binary the last element of the module path (or of main) The binary's name, in $MOORAGE_BIN. ldflags "-s -w" Linker flags. tags [] Build tags. cgo false Sets CGO_ENABLED; the server then needs a C compiler. The build is go build -trimpath -ldflags="…" -o "$MOORAGE_BIN/<binary>" <main>, and the web process runs the binary. See Go.
