[python] Key Default Description version .python-version, or else requires-python, or else the newest release Installed with uv; a partial version means its newest patch release. manager uv with a pyproject.toml, uv-pip with only a requirements.txt uv runs uv sync --locked --no-dev (uv sync --no-dev, with a warning, without a uv.lock); uv-pip makes a virtual environment and runs uv pip install -r requirements.txt. groups [] More dependency groups to install. extras [] Optional extras to install. The virtual environment's bin comes first on the PATH, and VIRTUAL_ENV and PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 are set. See Python. [node] Key Default Description version .nvmrc, or else .node-version, or else engines.node, or else the current LTS release Partial versions and ranges ("24", ">=22", "lts/*") mean the newest matching release. package_manager npm Only npm in this release: npm ci with a package-lock.json, npm install (with a warning) without one. build_script "build", when package.json has one The script run after the install. prune true Removes development dependencies after the build. The web process runs the start script directly, not through npm, so that the stop signal reaches the app; NODE_ENV=production is set. Without a start script, the build's dist/, build/ or out/ is served as a static site. See Node.js. [build] Key Default Description command the runtime's build Replaces the runtime's build. moor manifest explain shows the build it replaces. pre — Runs before the build (code generation, for instance). post — Runs after the build (a front end, for instance). env {} Variables for the build only. timeout "20m" The build fails after this long. exclude [] Patterns, in .gitignore syntax, removed from the build's output. Builds run in the directory the app will run from. The upload leaves out what .gitignore and .moorignore exclude, and node_modules, .venv and .git. [processes] Each entry is a long-running process. web receives the app's HTTP traffic. An entry is a command (worker = "python -m tasks.worker") or a table: Key Default Description command the runtime's, for web What to run. instances 1 How many instances run (0 to 20; 0 turns the process off). Requests are spread over the healthy ones. moor scale overrides it, on the server. expose true for web The process listens on $PORT (and $HOST). health a TCP check of $PORT See below. stop_signal "TERM" The signal that asks the process to stop: TERM, INT, QUIT, HUP, USR1 or USR2. stop_timeout "30s" How long the process may take to stop before it is killed. sleep true Whether it stops while its environment sleeps. restart "always" When an exited process is restarted: always, on-failure or never. Restarts slow down when a process keeps failing. protocol "http" For web, what it speaks on $PORT: http, or h2c for cleartext HTTP/2, which gRPC needs. sticky false For web, keeps a browser with the instance it first reached. See Scaling. health: Key Default Description path — An HTTP GET path; a 2xx or 3xx answer is healthy. Without it, a TCP connection to $PORT is the check. expect — Text the answer must contain. startup "60s" How long a new instance may take to become healthy during a deploy. interval "10s" Time between checks while the instance runs. timeout "3s" Each check's time limit. threshold 3 Failed checks in a row before an instance is unhealthy: it gets no traffic and is restarted. min_uptime "5s" For a process that does not listen: how long a new instance must keep running to count as healthy. Without [processes], a Procfile (name: command lines) is used, and then the runtime's own we

Every command of moor, as its --help says it. This page is made from the commands themselves, and a test keeps it the same as they are. The documentation lists the common ones. An app is chosen with --app, $MOOR_APP, [app].name in the moorage.toml of the current directory, or the repository's moorage git remote. Commands that talk to a server also take these, which are left out below: Flag What it says --server URL The server. By default $MOOR_SERVER, or the server configured on this machine --token TOKEN An API token. By default $MOOR_TOKEN, or the admin token of the server on this machine --ca-cert FILE A PEM file of an extra CA to trust, such as the server's internal CA. By default $MOOR_CA_CERT moor access Each environment has a gate, which applies to everything it serves: A share link works with every gate. A list of addresses can be combined with any of them. Unless one is set here, the gate is what the manifest asks, or else the server's default for that kind of environment. Flag Default What it does --app string app (default: $MOOR_APP or [app].name in moorage.toml) --env string production environment --json print as JSON moor access set Change an environment's gate, at once. default leaves it to the manifest and the server. The password gate asks for its password, without echoing it, or reads it from standard input. Changing the gate or its password ends everyone's way in. --allow-cidr replaces the list of addresses it can be reached from, and --anywhere takes the list away. Otherwise the list stays as it is. Flag Default What it does --allow-cidr strings addresses it can be reached from, such as 10.0.0.0/8 --any-user with login, let in anyone with an account --anywhere take away the list of addresses --app string app (default: $MOOR_APP or [app].name in moorage.toml) --env string production environment --password set the password too, for when the manifest asks for the gate moor agent Tell coding agents how to use Moorage moor agent init Add instructions for coding agents to the repository in DIR (default: the current directory): a section of AGENTS.md, and an Agent Skill in .agents/skills, .claude/skills and .kiro/skills. They teach an agent to deploy and look at this app with moor or moor mcp, and what to be careful of. They hold no token, so they can be committed. Running this again brings them up to date, and leaves the rest of AGENTS.md as it was. Flag Default What it does --app string the app; moorage.toml's name if left out moor alerts List an environment's thresholds. Past one for as long as it says, a notification goes to whoever a rule sends "A threshold is crossed" to, and another when it comes right. Flag Default What it does --app string app (default: $MOOR_APP or [app].name in moorage.toml) --env string production environment --json print JSON moor alerts add Add a threshold. METRIC is one of: A minute with no requests in it, or fewer than 5 for an error rate, says nothing either way. Flag Default What it does --app string app (default: $MOOR_APP or [app].name in moorage.toml) --env string production environment --for string 5m how long it has to go on for moor alerts rm Remove a threshold Flag Default What it does --app string app (default: $MOOR_APP or [app].name in moorage.toml) --env string production environment moor apps List the apps Flag Default What it does --json print as JSON moor apps create Create an app, before its first deployment. Deploying also creates one, in the default project: this is how an app starts in another. Flag Default What it does --project string the project it goes in (default: the default project) moor apps delete Delete an app: its instances, variables, releases, builds, logs and repository, and its data directory unless --keep-data keeps it. This cannot be undone. It asks you to type the app's name first, unless --yes. Flag Default What it does --keep-data keep its data directory --yes do not ask moor apps info Show an app's address and project, and how much room it takes Flag Default What it does --json print as JSON moor apps move Put an app in another project. It takes being a maintainer of both. Flag Default What it does --project string the project it goes in moor apps rename Give an app another name, which is another address and another git remote. Its instances stop and start again under the new name, so there is a moment of downtime. Change [app].name in its moorage.toml, and its git remote, to match: a deploy by the old name makes a new app. moor audit Show who did what, newest first: every change through the API or the console, every sign-in, every push and every secret revealed, whether it worked or not, kept for a year. It takes an administrator. Flag Default What it does --action string only actions with this text --actor string only what this person did --json print as JSON -n, --number int 50 how many, up to 200 --target string only what was done to this moor context A context is a server and the token for it, saved by moor login. Commands use the current one, unless --server or $MOOR_SERVER says otherwise. moor context rm Forget a context, without revoking its token moor context use Make a context the current one moor cron Cron jobs are declared in moorage.toml as [[cron]], and run as one-off instances of the current release. The last 100 runs of each are kept, with what they said. Flag Default What it does --app string app (default: $MOOR_APP or [app].name in moorage.toml) --env string production environment --json print as JSON moor cron log Show what a run said, and go on showing it until it ends Flag Default What it does --app string app (default: $MOOR_APP or [app].name in moorage.toml) moor cron run Run a cron job now, whatever its schedule says Flag Default What it does --app string app (default: $MOOR_APP or [app].name in moorage.toml) --detach start it and return --env string production environment moor cron runs List an environment's runs, newest first; a job's, if it is named Flag Default What it does -

Everything the command line does goes through the REST API, at /api/v1 on the console's hostname. openapi.json is its OpenAPI 3.1 document, also served by every server at /api/v1/openapi.json: every endpoint, its permission (x-moorage-permission), and its documents. Authentication Send an API token (Accounts and access) as a bearer token. Tokens are never accepted in a query string. A browser's session cookie works too. A cookie-authenticated request that changes anything must also send the session's CSRF token in X-CSRF-Token, and come from the console's own origin. Lists Lists that can grow come in pages, up to limit items (at most 200). Pass next_cursor back as cursor for the next page; there is none on the last. Running an app GET /api/v1/apps/{app}/envs/{env} says how an environment stands: its release, how many instances of each process it runs, and those instances. PATCH scales it, and answers the same, once it has got there; a new instance that cannot start leaves it as it was, with the code scale_failed: POST …/redeploy builds what the current release was built from again, and answers with the queued deployment, as a deploy does. GET …/releases/{version} has a release with its resolved manifest, and GET …/releases/{version}/diff/{other} what changed between two: of variables, their names only. Projects GET /api/v1/projects lists those you have a role in, and /projects/{project} has one with its apps and members. An app that you have no role with answers 404, as if it did not exist; one that your role does not allow answers 403, and says which role would. PUT and DELETE /projects/{project}/members/{user} change who is what, by email address or ID. POST /apps makes an app in a project, GET /apps/{app} says how much room it takes, PATCH /apps/{app} moves or renames it, and DELETE /apps/{app} removes it, with ?keep_data=true to keep its data directory. POST …/vars/{name}/reveal reads a secret, and is recorded, as is everything at GET /audit. Logs GET /api/v1/apps/{app}/envs lists its environments, and GET /api/v1/previews the previews of every app you can see, with when each expires. POST to /envs makes one, and to /previews one of a branch; POST /envs/{env}/promote, /lock and /unlock do what they say, and PATCH with pinned keeps a preview. GET and PUT /envs/{env}/access read and change who can reach it, and /envs/{env}/share-links makes, lists and with DELETE revokes links. GET /api/v1/apps/{app}/envs/{env}/logs streams an environment's logs as NDJSON, newest last: tail lines, then with follow=1 new ones as they come. source chooses from stdout, stderr, moorage, build, access and events; process, instance, grep, problems, since and until narrow them down. Each line has its source, and a level and message if it says. format=text sends plain text, and download=1 a file of up to 200,000 lines. A follower that reconnects says where it got to with after. What happened GET /api/v1/events lists what happened on the server, newest first, in pages, for an app and an env if given. GET /api/v1/events/stream follows it as server-sent events, each with the event's ID and, as its data, the same document. A reconnecting client says where it got to with the Last-Event-ID header, or ?after=, and is sent what it missed. A token restricted to an app sees only that app's. Events of a deployment.started kind are transient: they are for those following now, and are not kept. Errors Errors are RFC 9457 application/problem+json documents. code is stable, for programs; detail is for people; errors says what is wrong field by field. 401 means the credentials are missing or wrong, and 403 that they do not allow this. 429 comes with a Retry-After header. Stability Changes within v1 only add. A breaking change would be v2.

0.10.1 (2026-11-06) Moorage 0.10.1 fixes two things about stopping a server, for those who have more than one server on a machine, or use services. To upgrade from 0.10.0, run moor server upgrade. Running apps are taken over without a restart, and moor server upgrade --rollback goes back. This release does not change the database. Fixed moor server stop --all and moor server uninstall left services running, so that uninstalling Moorage could leave a database running that nothing looked after. They now stop them, after the apps, and what they hold stays in their volumes. The server starts them again when it next starts. --keep-apps leaves them running, as it does apps. moor server uninstall, start and restart went by the name of the service, and not by which server it runs. A server tried out with a configuration or a home directory of its own could take away the real one's service. They now leave it alone, as moor server stop already did. If yours was installed with a --config of its own, pass the same one, as they say if you do not. With engine = "auto" and both Podman and Docker installed, stopping everything only looked in the first. A server takes whichever answers, so that what it ran could be in the other. It now looks in both. moor server uninstall with no service said that it had removed one, and stopped the apps of a server that might be running without one. It now says that there is none, and leaves them. moor server stop --all stops them. 0.10.0 (2026-11-05) Moorage 0.10.0 runs a database for your app. Say [services.db] and type = "postgres" in moorage.toml, or type = "s3" for object storage, and each environment gets its own, with its address given to the app as it starts. They run in containers, so that they take Podman or Docker, and only those who use them need one. What this is not. In production, a service is one container with no replica, kept by backups: a convenience, and not database hosting. For a database that matters, set DATABASE_URL on production to one that is looked after, and let previews use their own. Apps on a machine are kept apart from a service by its password, and not by the network. Real PostgreSQL and object storage are tried under both engines in CI on Linux, and nowhere else: on macOS and Windows, a service's data lives inside the engine's machine, and goes with it. Everything before this that was untried still is: this release has not had an outside penetration test, or met Let's Encrypt itself, Cloudflare, or a webhook directly from GitHub, and setting up Kiro comes from its documentation alone. To upgrade from 0.9.0, run moor server upgrade. Running apps are taken over without a restart. This release changes the database, so that moor server upgrade --rollback puts the previous one back. Nothing about an app changes unless its manifest names a service, and a server that has none never asks for an engine because of them. Added [services.<name>], with type = "postgres", versions 15 to 18, or type = "s3", which is Versity Gateway on plain files, with one bucket and one key under the names that clients look for. Each environment and each preview has its own, with a random password. A service is made before a release, so that a release command can migrate, and one that does not become ready fails the deployment with the previous release still serving. Nothing is ever called latest. Previews are empty, unless you opt in. seed = "production" starts a new preview with production's latest dump, where nothing can connect until sanitize has run. That is refused for a preview anyone can reach, one from a fork, and one that a coding agent's token made. A later commit or moor access cannot open the gate over such a copy. A preview never ends up on production's database by inheritance. Sleep. An environment's services stop with it and keep what they hold, and waking starts them first. A command or a cron job starts what it needs for as long as it runs. Backups hold a dump of each service of production and of the named environments, made just before: pg_dumpall, or a tar of the object store. Volumes are not in a backup. After a restore to a new machine, a service loads its dump by itself before anything can connect to it. moor services restore goes back to the dump on the machine that it ran on, into a new volume, so that one that will not load changes nothing. moor services, with logs, update, upgrade --to, restore and remove. moor logs --service db reads what one has said. A new major version is refused at deploy, and moor services upgrade moves its data with the newer version's tools and checks that it holds what it did. After an upgrade or a restore, the old volume stays until --finish lets go of it, or --back goes back to it. A Services tab in the console, with what each has said and uses, and what an app's services add up to across its environments, as each preview has its own. What one uses is also in metrics, as service.db. moor server doctor says if one that should be running is not, and events say when one is made, restarted or removed. Changed A cold rootless Podman is given 15 seconds to answer for the first time, rather than 3, as that failed a first deployment. CI does not test the same code twice. A merge of a pull request that has passed takes about a minute, and the release of a commit that has passed reuses that. 0.9.0 (2026-11-05) Moorage 0.9.0 lets coding agents deploy to it and read how it went. moor mcp is a small server for Claude Code, Codex and others, which refuses a token that can do everything, and moor mcp setup makes a narrow one and connects a client. A token can be limited to previews, and moor agent init tells an agent how to use all of this. What that limit does not do. A token limited to previews reaches only the previews it makes, and is refused everything else, including what is added to Moorage later. Those previews take nothing of production's variables or those set for every environment. The code it deploys still runs on

Moorage is one program on one machine. This page says how it is put together, for whoever runs it, wants to know what it does before trusting it with something, or means to work on it. The design documents have a great deal more. One server process, a small supervisor for each native instance, and your apps. What runs Everything in the box above is one operating system process: the moor server. The only others Moorage starts are a small supervisor for each native instance, called a shim, which is the same binary in another mode; the apps; builds while they run; and, if you use containers, whatever the engine runs. Part What it does Ingress Answers HTTP and HTTPS. Matches the hostname and path to an environment, applies its gate, serves static files itself or passes the request to a healthy instance, wakes what sleeps, and counts what it does. API and console A JSON API under /api/v1, with streams for logs and events and a WebSocket for terminals, and a console of pages rendered by the server with a little plain JavaScript. Both are thin layers over the same code. The command line uses the API. Git server Takes pushes over SSH and HTTPS into bare repositories on disk, and shows the deployment to whoever pushed. Forges Listens for webhooks and looks for changes on GitHub, GitLab and Gitea, and reports back to them. Deployments A queue for each environment, recorded in the database, which turns source into a release: toolchains, build, release command, rollout. Toolchains Downloads Go, Node.js, uv and Python, checks them, and keeps them per version. Reconciler Compares what should be running with what is, and makes them match. The only part that starts and stops instances. Scheduler Cron jobs, sleep, the expiry of previews, the removal of old things, backups and roll-ups. Logs and metrics Log files, health checks and metrics, with notifications and telemetry on top. Store One SQLite database for everything that is a record, and plain files for everything else. Why apps survive the server Each native instance is started through a shim. The server starts the shim, in a session of its own, and the shim starts the app. The shim owns the app's output and writes it to its log, restarts the app if it exits, and answers the server on a loopback port with a secret of its own. It stays small: a few megabytes each. So when the server restarts, crashes or is upgraded, apps do not notice. As it starts, it finds its shims again from their state files, and takes them over before it opens its listeners, so that traffic goes on to the same instances. If a shim itself dies, its app is stopped with it, so that nothing is left running unknown, and the reconciler starts another. Containers need no shim, as the engine keeps them alive. They are labelled, so that the server finds them again. On Linux, the service unit lets the shims outlive the service, with Delegate=yes and KillMode=process, which is the arrangement container engines use. Stopping them all is a choice: moor server stop --all. What should be running The database says what should be running in each environment: its current release, how many instances of each process (none while it sleeps), its routes and gate, and its variables. The reconciler compares that with what is running, whenever something relevant happens and every 10 seconds regardless, and makes them match. A rollout is a short sequence of those states: add the new instances, wait until they are healthy, move the routes, finish, remove the old ones. A server that stops in the middle of one marks that deployment as failed when it comes back, and goes on with the current release, so that nothing is left half done. See How a release takes over. How things go A request to an app. The listener, then TLS, then a look at a routing table that is immutable and swapped whole, so that a request never sees half a change. Then the gate, then the static file, or the proxy to a healthy instance on 127.0.0.1. Then the response, and the metrics and access log. A git push. SSH or HTTP sign-in, then whether you may push to this app. The pack goes into the bare repository, each branch is matched to its environment, and its deployment runs, while its log goes back to you as git's progress messages. The branch is accepted or refused by how that went, so that a failed deploy is a failed push. A page of the console. The server renders it, with a session cookie and forms protected against forgery. A little JavaScript holds one connection to the event stream for live status, and a page out of sight lets go of it, and catches up when it returns. Where everything is The default locations are in Server configuration. In the data directory: You can look at all of it. ls a build, tail a log, and ps an app, as it is an ordinary process. High-volume data does not go through the database row by row: logs are files, and metrics are kept in memory and written in roll-ups. The database is SQLite, in WAL mode, with one writer and a few readers. Its migrations only go forward, and a copy is taken before any of them runs. A server refuses a database newer than it understands. Starting, stopping and upgrading Starting. Open and migrate the database, mark as failed what was interrupted, load the keys, take over shims and containers, rebuild the routing table, start the reconciler and scheduler, and only then open the listeners. Stopping. Finish the requests under way, interrupt builds, and exit, leaving apps running. What the metrics held in memory for the current minute is lost. Upgrading. moor server upgrade downloads the new release, checks it, and asks it what it is. It then keeps a copy of the database and of the binary, swaps the binary, and restarts the service. If the new version does not come up, it goes back by itself. Since the proxy, TLS and git server are compiled in, there are no separately versioned parts to drift apart. h: What it trusts, and what it does not
b: Moorage is meant for a team that trusts one another, on a network it controls, showing work to people outside it. This page says what it protects, how, and what it does not. The design document has more depth. Where this stands. Moorage is young, and has not had an outside security review. It has had close reviews of its own, the latest of what faces the internet and of what a low-privilege account can reach, and tests for what is described here, but no one has been paid to break it. A penetration test is on the roadmap. Until then, and whatever the public preset makes easy, keep it on a network you control, or behind something that decides who reaches it. What it trusts, and what it does not Who Trust An administrator Complete Runs the server, its users and settings A maintainer or deployer High Deploying is running code on the server. Give it as you would give someone a shell A viewer Some Sees status and metrics, and usually logs Someone visiting an app None Anyone who can reach the server An app and its dependencies Some May have bugs, or a compromised dependency Moorage does not contain someone who sets out to attack it from inside. A hostile deployer on a server with several teams is beyond what it is for: that takes separate machines. It is not a hosting service for strangers' code. Keeping apps apart What apps can do to one another depends on the system, and the level you choose: Linux, as root macOS Windows A user of its own for each app With user or sandbox No No Limited to its own files With sandbox No No Limits on memory and CPU Yes Memory, softly Yes Without a user of its own, apps can read one another's data and variables, and the server's database and master key, since they run as the account that holds them. The console says so on each app's page, and on the System page. For a shared server, use Linux, as root, with user or sandbox. Containers are another way to keep an app to itself: they run with no-new-privileges, with no host network, and rootless where the engine is. In every case, apps are told to listen on loopback, with HOST=127.0.0.1, so that they are reached through the server, and moor server doctor warns of one that can be reached another way. Other programs on the same machine can still reach them. Signing in Passwords are hashed with Argon2id, are at least 12 characters, and are checked against a list of common ones. Two-factor sign-in uses a time-based code from an app, with single-use codes and recovery codes. Single sign-on uses OpenID Connect, with group-to-role mapping, and can replace passwords. See How people sign in. Claiming a server takes a one-time code, so that nobody can race you to a new server on your network. Sessions are random, stored hashed, and expire. You can see and end yours. Tries are limited: on sign-in, by address and by account; on gate passwords, by address and environment; and on share links and SSH, by address. Failed sign-ins are logged, over the web and over SSH. API tokens start with moor_, so that scanners can find a leaked one. They are stored hashed, have scopes, and can be limited to one app and made to expire. They are never accepted in a query string. See Accounts and access. Secrets A secret is encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, under a key wrapped by the master key, and bound to its app, environment and name, so that a value cannot be moved to another variable. It is shown once, when set. A maintainer can reveal it, and that is recorded. It reaches an app in memory, and is on no command line or disk. A container's engine does keep it in the container's configuration, where those who can use the engine can read it. Its value is taken out of logs as they are captured, as far as it can be found there. Builds do not get secrets, unless you say so for each one. A backup leaves out the master key. Keep that safe and apart: with both, anyone can read the secrets, and without it, nobody can. The console and API The console has its own hostname, and its cookie goes nowhere else, so that an app cannot read it. Pages run under a strict Content-Security-Policy, with no inline scripts or styles, and cannot be framed. Requests that change something from a browser need a token bound to the session, and a same-origin request. A permission is declared for each route of the API, in one table, and a test goes through all of them for each kind of caller. A project can hide its apps from those with no role in it, who get the answer that an app that is not there gets. Accounts says where that stops. A token limited to one app reaches that app, and nothing of its project or of the others. One limited to previews reaches those, and changes only those that take nothing of production's. moor mcp gives coding agents little: nothing that runs a command, reads a secret or deletes anything. It refuses a token that can do everything. What this does not do is worth reading. moor server doctor and the System page warn of plain HTTP with no proxy in front, as credentials would travel unencrypted. Facing the internet Plain HTTP is redirected to HTTPS, and hsts, which the public preset turns on, tells browsers not to try it. A static site does not serve files or directories whose names start with a dot, except .well-known, unless it says to. So a .env or a .git left in the directory stays there. A request cannot pass itself off as the platform. Every spelling of X-Moorage-* is removed, as some ways of serving apps read X.Moorage.User and X_Moorage_User as the same header. What the server fetches Webhooks, mail servers, telemetry sinks and forges are named by people who may not run the server, so it refuses this machine, link-local addresses and clouds' metadata services for them, unless an administrator allows them in [notifications] allow. It checks as it connects, so that a name cannot resolve to one thing and then another, and follows no redirects.
